GR.w: In US style, the outer quotation uses double quotation marks, a quotation inside it uses single marks, and the period goes inside the closing marks.

n.0: In US style the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
n.1: This reverses US style, which puts double marks outside and single marks inside.
n.3: A quotation within a quotation takes single marks so the reader can tell where each ends.

GR.q: Which sentence about the patient's extra test is punctuated correctly?
o: The patient felt better; however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better, however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better however, the doctor ordered one more test.
The patient felt better; however the doctor ordered one more test.
GR.w: When a conjunctive adverb such as "however" joins two independent clauses, use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

n.1: Commas on both sides of "however" leave two independent clauses joined by commas, a comma splice.
n.2: With no punctuation before "however", the two independent clauses run together.
n.3: The comma after "however" is missing.

GR.q: Which sentence with a compound subject uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Neither the patient nor his daughters remembers the dosage.
The nurse and the respiratory therapist is reviewing the plan.
Macaroni and cheese is the side dish on every lunch tray today.
Either the aides or the charge nurse are bringing the blankets.
GR.w: "Macaroni and cheese" names one dish, a single unit, so it takes the singular verb "is."

n.0: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "daughters," so it must be "remember."
n.1: Two subjects joined by "and" are plural, so the verb must be "are reviewing."
n.3: With "either...or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "charge nurse," so it must be "is bringing."

GR.q: Which sentence uses "their," "there" and "they're" correctly?
o: Their leaving their coats over there by the door.
They're leaving their coats over their by the door.
They're leaving there coats over there by the door.
They're leaving their coats over there by the door.
GR.w: "They're" is the contraction of "they are", "their" shows possession (their coats), and "there" names a place (over there).

n.0: The sentence needs "they are leaving", so the contraction "they're" is required, not the possessive "their".
n.1: "Over ___" names a place, so "there" is required, not the possessive "their".
n.2: The coats belong to them, so the possessive "their" is required, not the place word "there".

GR.q: Which sentence uses "sit" and "set" correctly?
o: Please set in the chair by the window until your name is called.
The patient has set in the waiting room for over two hours.
She sat the specimen cup on the counter next to the sink.
He set the tray on the table and sat beside his mother.
GR.w: "Set" (set, set, set) means to place something and takes an object (the tray). "Sit" (sit, sat, sat) has no object (he sat).

n.0: A person resting in a chair needs "sit" (no object); "set" means to place something.
n.1: The patient is seated (no object), so the verb must be "sat": "has sat."
n.2: Placing a cup takes an object, so the verb must be "set": "She set the specimen cup."

GR.q: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence? "I am writing ___ your request for a copy of your records."
GR.w: The standard phrase is "in regard to" (or "with regard to"), with no s on "regard."

n.0: "In regard of" uses the wrong preposition; the phrase ends with "to."
n.1: "In regards to" is a nonstandard form; "regard" takes no s in this phrase.
n.3: "In regards of" adds an s and uses the wrong preposition.

GR.q: Which title for a patient handout uses standard title case?
o: A Guide To Caring For Patients In The Home
A guide to caring for patients in the home
a Guide to Caring for Patients in the Home
A Guide to Caring for Patients in the Home
GR.w: In title case, capitalize the first and last words and all major words (nouns, verbs, adjectives); lowercase articles and short prepositions in the middle (to, for, in, the).

n.0: Short prepositions (to, for, in) and articles (the) in the middle of a title are lowercase in title case.
n.1: This is sentence case; title case capitalizes the major words such as Guide, Caring, Patients and Home.
n.2: The first word of a title is always capitalized, even when it is an article.

GR.q: Which pair of words correctly completes the sentence? "Hospital ___ may not keep ___ belongings in the medication room."
GR.w: "Personnel" means staff; "personal" means belonging to a particular person.

n.1: The staff of a hospital are its "personnel," a noun.
n.2: Belongings that are one's own are "personal," not "personnel."
n.3: Both are reversed: staff are "personnel," and a person's own belongings are "personal."

GR.q: Which sentence about a faculty meeting is capitalized correctly?
o: The doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The Doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
The Doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
GR.w: A title is capitalized when it comes directly before a name (Professor Kim) but not when it is used as a general noun (the doctor).

n.0: A title used directly before a name is capitalized: "Professor Kim".
n.1: "Doctor" is used as a general noun after "the", not as a title before a name, so it is lowercase.
n.2: Both are reversed: the general noun is lowercase, and the title before a name is capitalized.

GR.q: In the sentence "Rosa drove home after her twelve-hour shift," what part of speech is the word "after"?
GR.w: "After" takes the noun phrase "her twelve-hour shift" as its object, with no verb, so it is a preposition.

n.0: "Twelve-hour" is the adjective; "after" links the noun phrase to "drove."
n.1: "After" is an adverb only with no object ("soon after"); here it has the object "shift."
n.3: A subordinating conjunction is followed by a subject and a verb ("after her shift ended"); here only a noun phrase follows.

GR.q: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence? "Ms. Park learned ___ about wound care during her first clinical rotation."
GR.w: "A lot" (a great deal) is written as two words.

n.1: "Alot" is not standard English; write "a lot."
n.2: "Allot" is a verb meaning to give out shares ("allot time"), which does not fit after "learned."
n.3: "Lot" stays singular in this phrase: "a lot," not "a lots."

GR.q: In the sentence "The aide handed the patient a cup of water," what is the function of "the patient"?
GR.w: "The patient" tells to whom the cup was handed, so it is the indirect object. "A cup" is the direct object: the thing handed.

n.0: A subject complement follows a linking verb; "handed" is an action verb.
n.1: The direct object receives the action: the aide handed "a cup," not the patient.
n.2: No preposition comes before "the patient"; with one, it would read "to the patient."

GR.q: Which sentence uses the pronoun "we" or "us" correctly?
o: The instructor gave us students extra time on the dosage exam.
Several of we applicants had questions about the essay prompt.
The new policy was explained to we volunteers on Monday.
Us students were asked to arrive by 6:30 a.m. for clinicals.
GR.w: Drop the noun to test: "The instructor gave us extra time" is correct, so "gave us students" is correct. "Us" is the indirect object of "gave."

n.1: "Of" is a preposition, so its object needs the objective case: "several of us applicants."
n.2: Drop "volunteers": "explained to we" is wrong. The object of "to" needs "us volunteers."
n.3: Drop "students": "Us were asked" is wrong. The phrase is the subject, so it must be "We students."

GR.q: Which sentence from a clinical narrative is free of a dangling modifier?
o: Walking into the clinic, the crowd in the lobby surprised her.
Walking into the clinic, it was clear that the lobby was full.
Walking into the clinic, Rosa saw that the lobby was crowded.
Walking into the clinic, the lobby looked crowded to Rosa.
GR.w: An introductory participial phrase must be followed by the person or thing doing the action. Rosa was walking into the clinic, so "Rosa" must come right after the comma.

n.0: The subject after the phrase is "the crowd," so the sentence says the crowd was walking into the clinic.
n.1: "It" cannot do the walking; the person who walked in never appears as the subject.
n.3: The phrase "Walking into the clinic" is followed by "the lobby," so the sentence says the lobby was walking.

GR.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? "Several of the cardiac monitors lost ___ signal during the storm last night."
GR.w: "Several" is always plural, so the plural possessive "their" agrees with it.

n.0: "Its" is singular, but "several" is plural.
n.1: "It's" means "it is" and is singular; the sentence needs a plural possessive.
n.3: "There" names a place; the sentence needs the possessive pronoun "their."

GR.q: Which line from a patient instruction sheet is a complete sentence?
o: Please sign the consent form before the procedure.
Signing the consent form before the procedure.
Since the consent form was signed before the procedure.
The consent form that was signed before the procedure.
GR.w: An imperative sentence is complete even though its subject (you) is not stated: "[You] Please sign the consent form."

n.1: This is a gerund phrase with no main verb.
n.2: "Since" makes this a dependent clause, which cannot stand alone.
n.3: "That was signed ..." is a relative clause describing the form; the subject "The consent form" has no main verb.

GR.q: Of the network's four sites, the downtown clinic is the one that schedules two nurses on weekends. Which sentence states this most clearly?
o: The downtown clinic only schedules two nurses on weekends.
The downtown clinic schedules only two nurses on weekends.
Only the downtown clinic schedules two nurses on weekends.
The downtown clinic schedules two nurses only on weekends.
GR.w: A limiting word such as only, just, nearly or almost goes directly before the word it limits. The point is that no other site does this, so "only" must come before "the downtown clinic."

n.0: Placed before the verb, "only" limits what the clinic does (or, loosely, the number); it never says that no other site does it.
n.1: Placed before "two nurses," "only" limits the number of nurses, not which site schedules them.
n.3: Placed before "on weekends," "only" limits the days: nurses are scheduled on weekends and not on weekdays.

GR.q: Which revision of "The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had been changed" makes the pronoun reference clear?
o: The pharmacist and the technician were told that her shift changed.
The pharmacist told the technician, "Your shift has been changed."
The pharmacist told the technician that her own shift had been changed.
The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had now been changed.
GR.w: Turning the report into a direct quotation makes "your" refer clearly to the technician, the person being spoken to.

n.0: "Her" now has two possible antecedents in the subject, so the reference is still unclear.
n.2: Adding "own" does not help: "her own" could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.
n.3: Adding "now" leaves "her" ambiguous; it could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.

GR.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The orientation leader asked ___ new hires to wait in the lobby."
GR.w: Drop the noun: "asked us to wait." The pronoun is the object of "asked," so the objective "us" is correct.

n.1: "Asked we" fails the drop test; "we" is subjective.
n.2: "Ourselves" is reflexive and needs "we" as the subject of the same clause.
n.3: "Them" cannot point to a noun; "them new hires" is nonstandard.

GR.q: Which sentence changes tense correctly because the time actually changes?
o: Last year Omar volunteered at the clinic, and now he works there.
Last year Omar has volunteered at the clinic, and now he works there.
Last year Omar volunteered at the clinic, and now he worked there.
Omar volunteers at the clinic last year, and now he works there.
GR.w: "Last year" calls for the past ("volunteered"), and "now" calls for the present ("works"): the tense changes because the time changes.

n.1: The present perfect "has volunteered" does not pair with the finished time "last year."
n.2: "Now" is present time, so the past "worked" is wrong.
n.3: "Last year" is past time, so the present "volunteers" is wrong.

GR.q: Which sentence about exam preparation avoids a shift in pronoun person?
o: If one studies daily, you will feel ready for the exam.
If students study daily, they will feel ready for the exam.
If students study daily, we will feel ready for the exam.
If a student studies daily, you will feel ready for the exam.
GR.w: "Students" and "they" are both third person plural, so person and number stay consistent.

n.0: The sentence shifts from third person ("one") to second person ("you").
n.2: The sentence shifts from third person ("students") to first person ("we").
n.3: The sentence shifts from third person ("a student") to second person ("you").

GR.q: Which sentence uses "bad" or "badly" correctly?
o: The new aide wrote the report bad and had to redo it.
The runner sprained her ankle bad during the race.
The patient's cough sounded bad last night.
The patient slept bad because of the noisy hallway.
GR.w: "Sounded" is a linking verb here: it connects the cough to a description, so it takes the adjective "bad."

n.0: "Wrote" is an action verb and needs the adverb "badly."
n.1: "Sprained" is an action verb and needs the adverb "badly."
n.3: "Slept" is an action verb and needs the adverb "badly."

GR.q: Jada has one sister-in-law, who owns a car. Which sentence correctly shows that the car belongs to that one sister-in-law?
o: My sisters-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister's-in-law car is in the shop.
My sister-in-law's car is in the shop.
My sister-in-laws car is in the shop.
GR.w: A compound noun forms its possessive on the last word: "sister-in-law's". The singular form is used because there is one owner.

n.0: "Sisters-in-law's" is the plural possessive, but Jada has only one sister-in-law.
n.1: The possessive ending goes on the last word of the compound, not the first.
n.3: "Sister-in-laws" has no apostrophe, so it is not a possessive.

GR.q: Which verb phrase correctly completes the sentence? "If the lab had called sooner, the nurse ___ the dose."
GR.w: A past condition contrary to fact uses "had" + past participle in the if-clause and "would have" + past participle in the result clause.

n.0: "Would of" is a mishearing of "would've"; "of" is not a verb.
n.2: "Had" + participle belongs in the if-clause; the result clause needs "would have changed."
n.3: "Will have changed" is the future perfect and cannot follow a past unreal condition.

GR.q: Which sentence about the crash cart contains an unnecessary preposition?
o: Where did you put the crash cart?
Where is the crash cart at right now?
The crash cart is next to the nurses' station.
Which room is the crash cart in?
GR.w: "Where" already means "at what place," so the "at" adds nothing: "Where is the crash cart right now?"

n.0: This question is correct and has no extra preposition.
n.2: "Next to" is needed to show location, so it is not extra.
n.3: "In" is needed to complete "in which room"; ending a sentence with a preposition is standard.

GR.q: Which sentence for a front-desk sign uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: There was several reasons that the appointment had to be moved.
Here is the signed consent forms for the two new patients.
There is two forms that every new patient must sign at check-in.
On the counter sit two charts that still need a provider's signature.
GR.w: When a sentence is inverted, find the subject after the verb. "Charts" is the subject of "sit," and both are plural, so "On the counter sit two charts" is correct.

n.0: The subject is "reasons" (plural), which comes after the verb, so it must be "There were."
n.1: The subject that follows the verb is "forms" (plural), so it must be "Here are the signed consent forms."
n.2: In a "there" sentence the subject follows the verb. The subject is "forms" (plural), so it must be "There are."

GR.q: Which sentence uses "rise" or "raise" correctly?
o: The patient's temperature rose overnight, so we called the doctor.
The therapist asked the patient to rise his arm above his head.
The aide raised from her chair when the surgeon entered the room.
Prices for the required nursing textbooks have raised every semester.
GR.w: "Rise" (rise, rose, risen) has no object; "raise" (raise, raised, raised) takes one. A temperature goes up by itself, so "rose" is correct.

n.1: Lifting an arm takes an object ("his arm"), so the verb must be "raise."
n.2: Getting up has no object, so the verb must be "rose" (past of "rise").
n.3: Prices go up on their own (no object), so the verb must be "risen": "have risen."

GR.q: Which sentence uses the articles "a" and "an" correctly?
o: The aide waited a hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited an hour before ordering a uniform.
The aide waited an hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering a uniform.
GR.w: The choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter: "an hour" (silent h, vowel sound) and "a uniform" (begins with a "you" consonant sound).

n.0: Both are reversed: "an hour" and "a uniform".
n.2: "Uniform" begins with a consonant "y" sound, so it takes "a".
n.3: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes "an".

GR.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? "The supervisor will give a parking pass to ___ needs one."
GR.w: Inside its own clause the pronoun is the subject of "needs" (he needs one), so "whoever" is correct. The whole clause "whoever needs one" is the object of "to."

n.0: "Whose" shows possession and would need a noun after it.
n.2: "Whomever" is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of "needs"; the preposition governs the whole clause, not the pronoun.
n.3: "Whom" is objective and cannot be the subject of "needs."

GR.q: In formal written English, which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly?
o: If I were the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I would be the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I was the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I will allow one retake per exam.
GR.w: For an unreal or hypothetical condition, formal English uses "were" for all subjects and "would" in the main clause.

n.1: "Would" belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause; use "If I were."
n.2: A condition contrary to fact takes the subjunctive "were" in formal writing, not "was."
n.3: An unreal "if I were" condition pairs with "would," not the future "will."

GR.q: Which sentence from a bonus notice uses possessive time expressions correctly?
o: The bonus equals one weeks pay for two weeks' work.
The bonus equals one week's pay for two week's work.
The bonus equals one weeks' pay for two weeks' work.
The bonus equals one week's pay for two weeks' work.
GR.w: Two steps: one week is singular, so add 's (one week's pay); two weeks is a plural ending in s, so add only an apostrophe (two weeks' work).

n.0: "One weeks pay" uses a plural with "one" and leaves out the apostrophe.
n.1: "Two weeks" is plural, so the apostrophe goes after the s: "weeks'".
n.2: "One week" is singular, so its possessive is "week's", not "weeks'".

GR.q: Which marks should enclose an interrupting phrase that already contains commas, to give it more emphasis than parentheses?
GR.w: A pair of dashes works like a pair of commas or parentheses but gives more emphasis, and it can enclose an element that has its own internal commas.

n.0: Brackets mark the writer's own insertions inside a quotation.
n.1: A colon introduces a list, explanation or quotation after an independent clause; colons are not used in pairs.
n.2: Semicolons join independent clauses or separate complex series items; they do not enclose interrupters.

GR.q: Which sentence about a wellness workshop uses hyphens correctly?
o: Twenty-one nurses joined the self care workshop this year.
Twenty one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the selfcare workshop this year.
Twenty-one nurses joined the self-care workshop this year.
GR.w: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated, and the prefix self- always takes a hyphen (self-care).

n.0: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, and the compound modifies the noun "workshop".
n.1: Compound numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine take a hyphen.
n.2: The prefix self- is joined with a hyphen, not closed up.

GR.q: Which revision corrects the agreement error in "Here's the forms that the new patient needs to sign before the exam"?
o: Here are the forms that the new patient needs to sign before the exam.
Here's the forms that the new patient need to sign before the exam.
Here are the forms that the new patient need to sign before the exam.
Here is the forms that the new patient needs to sign before the exam.
GR.w: The subject "forms" follows the verb and is plural, so "Here are" is needed. Inside the clause, "patient" is singular, so "needs" stays.

n.1: "Here's" is still "here is" with the plural "forms," and "patient need" adds a second agreement error.
n.2: "Here are" is fixed, but "the new patient need" breaks agreement; a singular subject takes "needs."
n.3: "Here is" is singular, but the subject that follows it, "forms," is plural.

GR.q: Which word in the sentence contains an error? "The mens' locker room and the women's lounge were repainted despite the residents' objections."
GR.w: "Men" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "men's".

n.0: "Objections" is a plain plural that owns nothing, so no apostrophe is needed.
n.2: "Residents'" is correct: a regular plural ending in s adds only an apostrophe.
n.3: "Women's" is correct: an irregular plural not ending in s adds 's.

GR.q: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly?
o: The surgeon finishes the procedure by the time the family had arrived.
The surgeon has finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrives.
The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
GR.w: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the earlier of two past actions. The procedure ended first, then the family arrived.

n.0: The tenses are reversed: the earlier action (finishing) needs the past perfect, and the later one the simple past.
n.1: The present perfect "has finished" does not fit a completed past time frame set by "arrived"; use "had finished."
n.2: "Arrives" is present tense, which clashes with "had finished"; both events are in the past.

GR.q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? "Several of the charts on the desk needs a signature before the patients go home."
GR.w: "Several" is an indefinite pronoun that is always plural, so the verb must be "need": "Several of the charts ... need a signature."

n.0: "Go" agrees with the plural subject "patients" in the clause "before the patients go home."
n.1: "Charts" is correctly plural as the object of "of"; it is not the subject of the verb.
n.3: "Several" is a correct plural subject here; the error is the singular verb that follows it.

GR.q: Which sentence uses the commonly confused words correctly?
o: All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
GR.w: "Except" means excluding (all except Mr. Ito); "lose" means to misplace (not to lose their wristbands). "Loose" means not tight.

n.0: Both are wrong: excluding someone is "except", and misplacing something is "lose".
n.1: "Accept" means to receive; excluding someone requires "except".
n.3: "Loose" is an adjective meaning not tight; misplacing something is "lose".

GR.q: In the sentence "Dr. Kim, the new cardiologist, starts on Monday," what is the function of "the new cardiologist"?
GR.w: "The new cardiologist" is a noun phrase set off by commas that renames "Dr. Kim," so it is an appositive.

n.0: A subject complement follows a linking verb ("Dr. Kim is the new cardiologist"); no linking verb comes before this phrase.
n.1: The subject is "Dr. Kim"; the phrase only renames the subject.
n.2: "Starts" takes no object here; the phrase sits beside the subject, not after the verb.

GR.q: Which sentence from a college brochure uses "not only...but also" correctly?
o: The program not only trains nurses but also places them in local clinics.
The program not only trains nurses but also it places them in local clinics.
Not only does the program train nurses but also places them in local clinics.
The program trains not only nurses but also places them in local clinics.
GR.w: Correlative pairs must be followed by matching elements. Here each part is followed by a verb phrase: "not only trains ... but also places."

n.1: "But also" is followed by a full clause ("it places"), while "not only" is followed by a verb; the two parts do not match.
n.2: "Not only" introduces an inverted clause, but "but also" introduces a bare verb phrase, so the pair is not parallel.
n.3: "Not only" precedes a noun ("nurses") but "but also" precedes a verb ("places"); each part needs the same form.

GR.q: Which sentence about the night shift is punctuated correctly?
o: After the power failed, the nurses used flashlights, but the monitors, kept running.
After the power failed, the nurses used flashlights, but the monitors kept running.
After the power failed, the nurses, used flashlights, but the monitors kept running.
After the power failed, the nurses used flashlights but, the monitors kept running.
GR.w: Two rules apply: a comma follows the introductory clause, and a comma goes before "but" when it joins two independent clauses.

n.0: A comma must not separate the subject "the monitors" from its verb "kept."
n.2: A comma must not separate the subject "the nurses" from its verb "used."
n.3: The comma belongs before the coordinating conjunction "but," not after it.

GR.q: Which sentence about the clinic's fees uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Forty dollars is the usual copay for a specialist visit.
The number of unpaid bills have dropped since January.
The news from the billing office were better than expected.
A number of patients has asked about the new payment plan.
GR.w: An amount of money treated as one sum is singular, so "Forty dollars is the usual copay" is correct.

n.1: "The number of" names one figure and is singular, so the verb must be "has dropped."
n.2: "News" ends in -s but is singular, so the verb must be "was."
n.3: "A number of" means "several" and is plural, so the verb must be "have asked."

GR.q: Which word in the sentence is an abstract noun? "The volunteer's patience comforted the frightened child."
GR.w: "Patience" names a quality you cannot see or touch, so it is an abstract noun.

n.0: "Child" is a concrete noun: a person you can see.
n.2: "Frightened" describes the child, so it is an adjective.
n.3: "Volunteer's" is the possessive form of a concrete noun, a person you can see.

GR.q: Which sentence uses "to," "too" and "two" correctly?
o: The two aides were too tired to finish the charts.
The two aides were to tired to finish the charts.
The two aides were too tired too finish the charts.
The too aides were too tired to finish the charts.
GR.w: "Two" is the number, "too" means excessively (too tired), and "to" begins the infinitive (to finish).

n.1: "___ tired" means excessively tired, which requires "too".
n.2: An infinitive is formed with "to": "to finish".
n.3: The number of aides requires "two".

MA.q: A hospital employs 250 nurses, and 38 of them hold a specialty certification. What percent of the nurses hold a specialty certification? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.0.152: Left the answer as a decimal instead of converting to a percent.
tr.84.8: Found the percent of nurses without a certification.

MA.q: A nursing program received 450 applications this year and accepted 18% of the applicants. How many applicants did the program accept?
MA.w: Part = percent × whole. 18% = 0.18, so 0.18 × 450 = 81 applicants.

n.1: This rounds 18% up to 20% before multiplying (0.20 × 450 = 90). Rounding is for estimating; the exact count uses 0.18.
n.2: This is the number of applicants who were not accepted (82%).
n.3: This divides 450 by 18 instead of multiplying 450 by 0.18.

MA.q: How much greater is 5.3 than 4.87?
MA.w: 5.30 - 4.87: borrow for the hundredths (10 - 7 = 3), then for the tenths (12 - 8 = 4), leaving 4 - 4 = 0 ones: 0.43. Check: 4.87 + 0.43 = 5.30.

n.0: 1.57 takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing.
n.2: 0.53 forgets to reduce the tenths digit after borrowing from it (13 - 8).
n.3: 1.43 forgets to reduce the ones digit after borrowing from it (5 - 4).

MA.q: An order is for 45 mg. The label reads 30 mg per 2 mL. Which proportion can be solved to find x, the number of milliliters to give?
MA.w: Keep mg over mL on both sides: 30 mg/2 mL = 45 mg/x mL. Cross-multiply: 30x = 90, so x = 3 mL.

n.0: This writes mL over mg on the left but mg over mL on the right, giving x = 675.
n.2: This pairs the ordered 45 mg with the 2 mL that holds 30 mg, giving x = 1.33.
n.3: This puts the second ratio upside down (mL over mg), giving x = 675.

MA.q: A unit stocks 30 IV poles, and 12 are in use. Which fraction is equivalent to 12/30?
MA.w: 12/30 simplifies by its GCF, 6, to 2/5. 14/35 also simplifies to 2/5 (divide both terms by 7). Check by cross-multiplying: 12 × 35 = 420 and 30 × 14 = 420.

n.0: 14/32 adds 2 to the top and the bottom; adding does not keep the value (14/32 = 7/16).
n.1: 4/6 divides 12 by 3 but 30 by 5; 4/6 = 2/3, not 2/5.
n.3: 6/10 divides 12 by 2 but 30 by 3; 6/10 = 3/5, not 2/5.

MA.q: A wound is 6.35 cm long. What is its length in inches?
MA.w: Centimeters to inches: divide by 2.54. 6.35 ÷ 2.54 = 2.5 in. Check: 2.5 × 2.54 = 6.35 cm.

n.0: This divides by 2.2, the pounds-per-kilogram factor (6.35 ÷ 2.2 = 2.9).
n.2: This multiplies by 2.54; inches are larger than centimeters, so the number must get smaller.
n.3: This divides by 25.4, the number of millimeters in an inch, but the length is in centimeters.

MA.q: A baker mixes flour, sugar and butter in the ratio 5:2:3 by weight. She uses 12 ounces of sugar. How many ounces of butter does she use?
MA.w: Sugar is 2 parts, so one part = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 ounces. Butter: 3 × 6 = 18 ounces.

n.1: This is the amount of flour (5 parts), not butter.
n.2: This scales the wrong way, multiplying 12 by 2/3 instead of by 3/2.
n.3: This is the total weight of all three ingredients (10 parts).

MA.q: A medical assistant's hourly wage rose from $18.40 to $20.70. What was the percent increase in the hourly wage? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.11.11: Divided the $2.30 raise by the new wage, $20.70, instead of the original wage.
tr.2.3: Reported the dollar increase instead of the percent increase.

MA.q: A solution contains 2 g of a drug in 500 mL. How many milligrams of the drug are in 1 mL?

n.0: This divides 500 by 2, which gives milliliters per gram, not milligrams per milliliter.
n.2: This changes 2 g to 200 mg (× 100) before dividing by 500.
n.3: 0.004 is the amount in grams per mL (2 ÷ 500); it was not changed to milligrams.

MA.q: A hospital department logged 2,749.5 overtime hours last year. What is 2,749.5 rounded to the nearest hundred?
MA.w: The hundreds digit is 7. Look only at the digit to its right (tens), which is 4, so keep 7: 2,700.

n.0: 2,800 rounds in two steps (2,749.5 → 2,750 → 2,800). Round once, using the tens digit.
n.2: 2,750 rounds to the nearest ten, not the nearest hundred.
n.3: 3,000 rounds to the nearest thousand.

MA.q: At 6 a.m. the outdoor temperature in Fargo was -7°F. By noon it had risen 15 degrees, and by 9 p.m. it had fallen 11 degrees from the noon reading. What was the temperature at 9 p.m.?
MA.w: Start at -7, add the rise and subtract the fall: -7 + 15 = 8, then 8 - 11 = -3°F.

n.0: 11°F treats the starting temperature as +7 (7 + 15 - 11).
n.1: 19°F adds the 11-degree fall instead of subtracting it (8 + 11).
n.2: 3°F drops the negative sign; 8 - 11 is 3 below zero.

MA.q: Evaluate 18 - 6 ÷ 3 × 2 + 4.
MA.w: Multiplication and division have equal rank, so work left to right: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, then 2 × 2 = 4. Then add and subtract left to right: 18 - 4 = 14, and 14 + 4 = 18.

n.0: 12 works strictly left to right from the start (18 - 6 first), ignoring that division and multiplication come before subtraction.
n.1: 21 multiplies 3 × 2 before dividing (6 ÷ 6 = 1); division comes first here because it is on the left.
n.3: 10 adds 4 + 4 before subtracting; addition and subtraction are done left to right.

MA.q: A child who weighs 18 kilograms is prescribed a medication at 15 milligrams per kilogram per day, divided into 3 equal doses. How many grams of the medication are in each dose? Enter your answer in grams.

tr.90: Stopped at milligrams; the question asks for grams.
tr.0.27: Gave the full daily amount (270 mg = 0.27 g) instead of one of the 3 doses.

MA.w: Daily amount = 15 mg × 18 = 270 mg. Each dose = 270 ÷ 3 = 90 mg. Milligrams to grams: divide by 1,000, so 90 mg = 0.09 g.

MA.q: An IV infusion pump delivers fluid at a constant rate of 125 milliliters per hour. If the rate is not changed, how many liters of fluid will the patient receive during a 12-hour shift?

n.0: This divides 1,500 mL by 100 instead of 1,000.
n.1: This divides 1,500 mL by 10,000 instead of 1,000.
n.3: This is the amount for one hour (125 mL); multiply by the 12 hours first.

MA.q: A clinic can buy exam gloves in a box of 100 for $8.40 or in a case of 10 such boxes for $76.50. How much is saved per glove by buying the case instead of single boxes?
MA.w: Single box: $8.40 ÷ 100 = $0.084 per glove. Case: $76.50 ÷ 1,000 = $0.0765 per glove. Savings: 0.084 - 0.0765 = $0.0075 per glove, which is 0.75 cent.

n.1: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 cent; this moves the decimal one place too far.
n.2: This is the savings per box of 100 gloves ($8.40 - $7.65), not per glove.
n.3: Decimal slip: $0.0075 is 0.75 of a cent, not 7.5 cents.

MA.q: A medication is ordered at 15 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, divided into 3 equal doses. A child weighs 44 pounds. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams should be given in each dose?
MA.w: Weight: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. Daily dose: 15 × 20 = 300 mg. Each dose: 300 ÷ 3 = 100 mg.

n.0: This is the total daily dose; it must be divided into 3 equal doses.
n.2: This uses the weight in pounds and also gives a daily total, 44 × 15.
n.3: This uses the weight in pounds (44 × 15 ÷ 3) instead of converting to 20 kg first.

MA.q: A textbook has 320 pages. Ana has read 3/8 of it, and Ben has read 2/5 of it. How many more pages has Ben read than Ana?

n.0: 248 adds both readers' pages; "how many more" needs a subtraction.
n.2: 128 is the number of pages Ben has read, not the difference.
n.3: 120 is the number of pages Ana has read, not the difference.

MA.q: A patient must take 2 tablets three times a day for 14 days and already has 25 of these tablets at home. More tablets are sold only in bottles of 30. How many bottles must be purchased to complete the full course?
MA.w: Tablets needed: 2 × 3 × 14 = 84. Subtract the 25 at home: 84 - 25 = 59. Bottles: 59 ÷ 30 = 1.97. One bottle is not enough, so round up to 2 bottles (60 tablets, enough for the 59 still needed).

n.0: 1 bottle rounds 1.97 down; 30 + 25 = 55 tablets would run out before the 84 needed.
n.1: 3 bottles ignores the 25 tablets at home (84 ÷ 30 = 2.8, rounded up), so it buys one bottle too many.
n.2: 4 bottles adds the 25 tablets at home to the 84 needed (109 ÷ 30 = 3.63) instead of subtracting them.

MA.q: A rideshare driver is paid $3 for each trip plus $1.25 for every mile of the trip. Which expression gives the driver's pay, in dollars, for a single trip that is m miles long?
MA.w: Total = fixed amount + rate × quantity. The fixed amount is $3 per trip and the rate is $1.25 per mile, so the pay is 1.25m + 3 dollars.

n.0: 1.25m and 3 are not like terms, so they cannot be combined; 4.25m would pay $4.25 for every mile.
n.1: This multiplies the $3 trip payment by 1.25 as well, which gives 1.25m + 3.75 instead of adding a flat $3.
n.3: This swaps the two amounts: $3 is the flat payment per trip, and $1.25 is the rate that multiplies the miles.

MA.q: A medical equipment sales representative earns a base salary of $2,100 per month plus a 6% commission on her monthly sales above $15,000. In May her sales totaled $38,500. What was her total pay for May?

n.0: This pays the 6% commission on all $38,500 of sales instead of on the $23,500 above $15,000.
n.1: This is the commission alone; her base salary of $2,100 must be added.
n.3: This is 6% of all $38,500 in sales, without the base salary and without excluding the first $15,000.

MA.q: It takes 3 aides 8 hours to restock all of a hospital's supply rooms. Working at the same rate, how long would it take 4 aides to do the same job?
MA.w: This is an inverse proportion: aides × hours stays constant. 3 × 8 = 24 aide-hours, so 4 aides need 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.

n.0: This treats the relationship as direct. More aides finish faster, so the time must decrease.
n.1: This divides the original 8 hours by 4 aides and ignores that the 8 hours was for 3 aides.
n.2: This subtracts 1 hour for the 1 extra aide. The total work, 24 aide-hours, stays the same.

MA.q: Write 909 in Roman numerals.
MA.w: 900 = CM and 9 = IX. Together: CMIX.

n.0: I may not repeat four times; 9 is written IX.
n.1: CMXI = 900 + 11 = 911; 9 is IX, with the I first.
n.2: C may not repeat four times; 900 is written CM.

MA.q: A bottle holds 8 fl oz of cough syrup. Each dose is 2 teaspoons. How many full doses does the bottle hold?
MA.w: 8 fl oz × 2 tbsp/fl oz × 3 tsp/tbsp = 48 tsp. 48 ÷ 2 = 24 doses. (Or 8 × 30 mL = 240 mL ÷ 10 mL = 24.)

n.1: 48 is the number of teaspoons in the bottle; each dose uses 2.
n.2: This treats each 2-teaspoon dose as 2 tablespoons (16 tbsp ÷ 2 = 8).
n.3: This uses 3 teaspoons per fluid ounce (24 tsp ÷ 2); 1 fl oz = 6 tsp.

MA.q: A drug label lists 37 1/2% of a dose as the starting amount. Which fraction, in lowest terms, is equal to 37 1/2%?

n.1: 1/3 is the benchmark for 33 1/3%, not 37 1/2%.
n.2: 37/100 drops the 1/2 percent; 37/100 = 37%.
n.3: 3/80 = 0.0375, which is 3.75%; the decimal point was moved one place too far.

MA.q: A medication is ordered at 2 mg per minute. The solution contains 500 mg in 250 mL. At how many milliliters per hour should it run?
MA.w: Strength: 500 mg ÷ 250 mL = 2 mg per mL. Per minute: 2 mg ÷ 2 mg per mL = 1 mL. Per hour: 1 × 60 = 60 mL per hour.

n.0: This is the rate per minute; there are 60 minutes in an hour.
n.1: This is the dose in milligrams per hour (2 × 60), not milliliters.
n.2: This inverts the strength, using 0.5 mg per mL (250 ÷ 500).

MA.q: A vaccine refrigerator log lists a reading of 41 °F. The clinic's storage policy lists temperature limits in degrees Celsius. What is the refrigerator's temperature in degrees Celsius?

n.1: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.
n.2: This multiplies 41 by 5/9 without first subtracting 32.
n.3: This multiplies by 5/9 and then subtracts 32; subtract 32 first.

MA.q: A patient's temperature falls from 102.2 °F to 99.5 °F. By how many degrees Celsius did the temperature fall?
MA.w: The fall is 2.7 °F. A change of 1 °F is 5/9 of a Celsius degree, so 2.7 × 5/9 = 1.5 °C. Check: 102.2 °F = 39 °C and 99.5 °F = 37.5 °C; 39 - 37.5 = 1.5.

n.0: This applies the 5/9 factor twice (1.5 × 5/9 = 0.8).
n.1: 2.7 is the fall in Fahrenheit degrees; it still has to be multiplied by 5/9.
n.2: This multiplies the 2.7 °F change by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

MA.w: Innermost first: 4 + 2 = 6, and 6² = 36. Brackets: 20 - 36 = -16. Then 3 × (-16) = -48, and -48 ÷ 4 = -12.

n.0: 0 squares each term separately (16 + 4 = 20), so the brackets become 20 - 20.
n.1: -48 is 3 × (-16), one step short: the division by 4 has not been done.
n.3: 51 multiplies only the 20 by 3 and divides only the 36 by 4: 60 - 9.

MA.q: During one shift, a patient drinks 2 cups of broth, 6 fluid ounces of juice, and 3 tablespoons of a liquid supplement. Use 1 cup = 240 milliliters. What is the total intake? Enter your answer in milliliters.

tr.675: Used 5 mL (a teaspoon) for each tablespoon.
tr.750: Counted each tablespoon as 1 fluid ounce (30 mL); 1 tbsp = 15 mL.

MA.w: Broth: 2 × 240 = 480 mL. Juice: 6 × 30 = 180 mL. Supplement: 3 × 15 = 45 mL. Total = 480 + 180 + 45 = 705 mL.

MA.q: A pediatric unit has 3 nurses for every 8 patients. Which ratio compares the patients to all the people (nurses and patients) on the unit?
MA.w: Each group of 3 nurses and 8 patients has 3 + 8 = 11 people. Patients to all people: 8:11.

n.0: This is patients to nurses, a part-to-part ratio. The question asks for patients to everyone.
n.1: This reverses the order: all people to patients.
n.3: This is nurses to all people. The question asks for patients first.

MA.q: Four IV bags have 5/7, 0.71, 0.705 and 7/10 of their volume left. Which amount is greatest?
MA.w: Convert and pad to four places: 5/7 = 0.7142..., 0.71 = 0.7100, 0.705 = 0.7050 and 7/10 = 0.7000. The greatest is 5/7.

n.0: 7/10 = 0.7000, the least of the four values.
n.1: 0.71 = 0.7100 is less than 5/7 = 0.7142...; divide 5 by 7 to at least three places before comparing.
n.3: 0.705 has the most digits, but 0.7050 is less than 0.7100 and 0.7142...

MA.q: A clinic closes for lunch at 12:15 p.m. and reopens at 1:20 p.m. Which pair gives these times in military time?
MA.w: The noon hour stays as written: 12:15 p.m. = 1215. For 1:20 p.m., add 12: 1320.

n.0: This writes the noon hour as 00 and does not add 12 to 1:20 p.m.
n.1: 1215 is right, but 1:20 p.m. needs 12 added: 1320, not 0120.
n.2: Nothing is added to the noon hour; 12:15 p.m. is 1215.

MA.q: Of the 640 students in a prerequisite course, 45% are taking the HESI A2 this semester, and 75% of those students plan to apply to a BSN program. How many students in the course plan to apply?
MA.w: Taking the HESI A2: 0.45 × 640 = 288. Planning to apply: 0.75 × 288 = 216. (Equivalently, 0.45 × 0.75 = 0.3375 and 0.3375 × 640 = 216.)

n.1: This is the number taking the HESI A2; 75% of those 288 students still has to be found.
n.2: This takes 75% of all 640 students instead of 75% of the 288 taking the HESI A2.
n.3: This subtracts the percents (75% - 45% = 30%) and takes 30% of 640. A percent of a percent is found by multiplying.

MA.q: A child takes 1/2 teaspoon of a liquid vitamin three times a day for 10 days. The oral syringe that comes with the bottle is marked in milliliters. How many milliliters of the vitamin will the child take over the 10 days?

n.0: This uses 15 mL per teaspoon, which is the tablespoon amount (7.5 mL per dose).
n.1: This is one day's amount (3 × 2.5 mL); the course lasts 10 days.
n.3: This uses a full teaspoon (5 mL) per dose instead of 1/2 teaspoon.

MA.q: Of the 30 students in a nursing assistant class, 18 passed the skills test on the first attempt. What is the ratio of students who passed to students who did not, in lowest terms?
MA.w: Students who did not pass: 30 - 18 = 12. Passed to did not pass: 18:12. Divide both by 6: 3:2.

n.0: This compares those who passed with the whole class (18:30), a part-to-whole ratio.
n.1: This compares the whole class with those who passed (30:18).
n.2: This reverses the order: it compares students who did not pass with those who passed.

MA.q: Write 7/12 as a decimal rounded to the nearest hundredth.
MA.w: 7 ÷ 12 = 0.58333... The thousandths digit is 3, so round down: 0.58.

n.0: 0.84 multiplies 7 × 12 instead of dividing 7 by 12.
n.2: 1.71 divides the denominator by the numerator (12 ÷ 7).
n.3: 0.60 rounds to the nearest tenth (0.6) first and then adds a zero; that is rounding too early.

MA.q: A prescriber orders 0.15 mg of a drug for each kilogram of body weight. The patient weighs 72.6 kg. What is the dose? Do not round until the final answer, and round it to the nearest tenth of a milligram. Enter the number only.

tr.11: Rounded the weight to 73 kg first (0.15 × 73 = 10.95, which rounds to 11.0).

MA.w: Dose = 0.15 × 72.6 = 10.89 mg. Round only at the end: the hundredths digit is 9, so 10.89 → 10.9 mg.

MA.q: Solve for x: -3(2x + 5) = 21.
MA.w: Distribute: -6x - 15 = 21. Add 15 to both sides: -6x = 36. Divide by -6: x = -6. Check: -3(2(-6) + 5) = -3(-7) = 21.

n.1: Sign error in the last step: -6x = 36 gives x = 36 ÷ (-6), which is negative.
n.2: This multiplies only the 2x by -3, giving -6x + 5 = 21, so -6x = 16.
n.3: This subtracts 15 instead of adding it: -6x - 15 = 21 gives -6x = 36, not -6x = 6.

MA.q: A patient has a fluid allowance of 1,200 mL for the day. She uses 1/4 of the allowance at breakfast, and then 2/3 of the remaining amount over lunch and dinner. How many milliliters are left for the evening?
MA.w: Breakfast: 1/4 × 1,200 = 300 mL, leaving 900 mL. Lunch and dinner: 2/3 × 900 = 600 mL, leaving 900 - 600 = 300 mL for the evening.

n.0: This is the amount left after breakfast, an intermediate step; lunch and dinner still have to be subtracted.
n.2: This is the amount used at lunch and dinner, not the amount left.
n.3: This takes 2/3 of the full 1,200 mL instead of 2/3 of the 900 mL remaining after breakfast.

MA.q: A patient takes 0.25 mg of a drug 3 times a day for 14 days. How many milligrams does the patient take in all?

n.0: 31.5 mg multiplies by 3 twice: the daily 0.75 mg already includes the 3 doses.
n.1: 3.5 mg counts one dose a day (0.25 × 14).
n.2: 1.05 mg places the decimal point one place too far left in 0.75 × 14.

MA.q: A soup recipe that serves 6 people uses 2 1/4 cups of broth. How many cups of broth are needed to make the recipe serve 10 people?
MA.w: Set up 2.25/6 = x/10. Cross-multiply: 6x = 22.5, so x = 3.75 = 3 3/4 cups.

n.0: This adds 4 cups for the 4 extra servings instead of scaling by 10/6.
n.2: This doubles the recipe, but 10 servings is 10/6 = 1 2/3 times the recipe, not 2 times.
n.3: This sets up the proportion upside down, multiplying 2 1/4 by 6/10.

MA.q: A courier charges 3 times the sum of a package's weight w, in pounds, and 2, plus a $5 handling fee. Which expression gives the charge, in dollars, for one package?
MA.w: 'The sum of w and 2' is (w + 2). '3 times the sum' is 3(w + 2). Adding the $5 handling fee gives 3(w + 2) + 5, which simplifies to 3w + 11.

n.0: This multiplies only w by 3. 'Times the sum' needs parentheses so both w and 2 are tripled: 3(w + 2) = 3w + 6.
n.1: This swaps the multiplier and the fee: the sum is multiplied by 3, and the $5 fee is then added.
n.2: This puts the $5 fee inside the parentheses, so the fee is tripled too. The fee is added once, after multiplying.

MA.q: Evaluate 36 ÷ 4 × 3 - 2².
MA.w: Exponent: 2² = 4. Divide and multiply left to right: 36 ÷ 4 = 9, 9 × 3 = 27. Subtract: 27 - 4 = 23.

n.0: -1 multiplies 4 × 3 before dividing (36 ÷ 12 - 4); division is on the left, so it goes first.
n.1: 9 subtracts 3 - 2 before squaring and multiplying; subtraction comes last.
n.2: 625 works left to right and squares last: (27 - 2)².

MA.q: A patient's fluid intake on Tuesday was 7/4 of the daily target set by the care team. Which percentage of the target did the patient take in?
MA.w: 7 ÷ 4 = 1.75. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 1.75 × 100 = 175%. A value greater than 1 is more than 100%.

n.0: 1.75% puts a percent sign on 1.75 without multiplying by 100.
n.1: 17.5% = 0.175. The decimal point in 1.75 was moved only 1 place right.
n.2: 57.1% is 4 ÷ 7, the reciprocal of 7/4.

MA.q: A nurse charted four times. Which entry is converted correctly?
MA.w: 3:20 p.m.: add 12 to the hour, 3 + 12 = 15, so 1520.

n.0: 12:10 a.m. is in the midnight hour, so it is 0010; 1210 is 12:10 p.m.
n.2: 12 is added to p.m. hours only; 6:05 a.m. is 0605.

MA.q: Which is the standard Roman numeral for 1,999?
MA.w: 1,000 = M, 900 = CM, 90 = XC, 9 = IX. Together: MCMXCIX.

n.0: I may be subtracted only from V or X, never from M.
n.2: C may not repeat four times; 900 is written CM.
n.3: IC for 99 is not standard; I may be subtracted only from V or X, so 99 is XCIX.

MA.q: During a quality check, 5 out of every 16 IV bags sampled had a label printed off-center. What percent of the sampled bags had an off-center label? Enter the number only, without the percent sign.

tr.3.125: Moved the decimal point only 1 place right.
tr.0.3125: Left the answer as a decimal instead of converting to a percent.

MA.w: 5/16 = 5 ÷ 16 = 0.3125. Multiply by 100 to write it as a percent: 0.3125 × 100 = 31.25, so 31.25%.

MA.q: A clinic orders 24 boxes of exam gloves listed at $8.75 per box. The supplier takes $0.50 off the price of each box. What is the total cost of the order?
MA.w: Discounted price per box: $8.75 - $0.50 = $8.25. Total: 24 × $8.25 = $198.00.

n.0: $209.50 takes $0.50 off the whole order instead of off each box.
n.2: $208.80 reads the discount as $0.05 per box ($8.70 × 24).
n.3: $210.00 is 24 × $8.75, the cost before the discount.

MA.q: Which fraction is less than 5/12?

n.0: 3/7 ≈ 0.429 is greater than 5/12 ≈ 0.417 (cross products 36 > 35).
n.2: 4/9 ≈ 0.444 is greater than 5/12 (cross products 48 > 45).
n.3: 7/16 = 0.4375 is greater than 5/12; its larger denominator does not make it smaller.

MA.q: A dietitian has 5 cups of yogurt. Each serving is 2/3 cup. How many full servings can be made?
MA.w: 5 ÷ 2/3 = 5 × 3/2 = 15/2 = 7 1/2 servings. Only full servings count, so the answer is 7. Check: 7 × 2/3 = 14/3 = 4 2/3 cups, with 1/3 cup left over.

n.0: 3 1/3 multiplies 5 by 2/3 instead of dividing by it.
n.1: 8 rounds 7 1/2 up, but 8 servings would need 5 1/3 cups.
n.3: 7 1/2 is the exact quotient; the half serving is not a full serving.

MA.q: A 12 3/4-foot length of tubing is cut into 4 equal pieces. How long is each piece, in feet?

n.0: 3 3/4 divides only the whole number (12 ÷ 4 = 3) and keeps the 3/4 unchanged.
n.1: 12 3/16 divides only the fraction part (3/4 ÷ 4 = 3/16) and keeps the 12.
n.2: 4 1/4 divides by 3, the number of cuts, instead of by 4, the number of pieces.

MA.q: What is the value of (-3) × 4 × (-2) × (-1) ÷ (-6)?
MA.w: Multiply left to right: (-3)(4) = -12; (-12)(-2) = 24; (24)(-1) = -24. Then -24 ÷ (-6) = 4. There are four negative signs (an even number), so the result is positive.

n.0: -4 miscounts the negative signs; there are four negatives, an even number, so the result is positive.
n.1: 144 multiplies -24 by -6 instead of dividing.
n.2: -144 multiplies by -6 instead of dividing and also miscounts the signs.

MA.w: Convert to improper fractions: 4 1/2 = 9/2 and 2 2/3 = 8/3. Multiply: 9/2 × 8/3 = 72/6 = 12. Cross-cancel check: (3/1) × (4/1) = 12.

n.0: 1 11/16 divides 9/2 by 8/3 (9/2 × 3/8 = 27/16) instead of multiplying.
n.2: 8 1/3 multiplies the whole numbers (4 × 2) and the fractions (1/2 × 2/3) separately.
n.3: 7 1/6 adds the two mixed numbers instead of multiplying them.

MA.q: Each tablet of a medication contains 0.125 mg of the active drug. A patient takes 2.5 tablets each day. How many milligrams of the drug does the patient take each day?
MA.w: Multiply: 125 × 25 = 3,125. The factors have 3 + 1 = 4 decimal places in total, so the product is 0.3125 mg.

n.0: 3.125 mg places the decimal point after only 3 decimal places; the factors have 4 in total.
n.2: 0.03125 mg uses 5 decimal places; the factors have 4 in total.
n.3: 0.05 mg divides 0.125 by 2.5 instead of multiplying.

MA.q: During a 12-hour shift, a nurse spends 1/6 of the time on breaks and charting, and 3/4 of the remaining time with patients. How many hours does she spend with patients?
MA.w: Breaks and charting: 1/6 × 12 = 2 hours, leaving 10 hours. With patients: 3/4 × 10 = 30/4 = 7 1/2 hours.

n.0: 9 takes 3/4 of the full 12 hours instead of 3/4 of the 10 hours remaining.
n.1: 2 1/2 is the time left after patient care (10 - 7 1/2), not the time with patients.
n.3: 10 is the time remaining after breaks and charting, one step short of the answer.

AP.q: Which glands secrete an oily substance, usually into hair follicles, that softens skin and hair, slows water loss and helps inhibit bacterial growth?
AP.w: Sebaceous (oil) glands secrete sebum, usually into hair follicles. Sebum lubricates and softens skin and hair, slows water loss and is antibacterial. They are absent from the palms and soles.

n.1: Ceruminous glands are modified sweat glands that produce earwax in the ear canal.
n.2: Apocrine glands also open into hair follicles, but they secrete a thicker sweat, not oily sebum.
n.3: Eccrine glands open onto the skin surface through pores and secrete watery sweat.

AP.q: During micturition, which structure contracts to push urine out of the urinary bladder and into the urethra?
AP.w: The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall. In micturition it contracts while the internal (involuntary, smooth) and external (voluntary, skeletal) urethral sphincters relax, so urine flows into the urethra.

n.0: The internal urethral sphincter relaxes during micturition so urine can leave; it holds urine in rather than expelling it.
n.2: Ureteral smooth muscle moves urine from the kidneys into the bladder by peristalsis; it does not empty the bladder.
n.3: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle that is voluntarily relaxed to allow urination; it does not push urine out.

AP.q: A patient has intense thirst and passes very large volumes of dilute urine, but his blood glucose is normal. A deficiency of which hormone, from which gland, best explains this?
o: Aldosterone released from the adrenal medulla
Insulin released from the pancreatic beta cells
ADH released from the anterior pituitary
ADH released from the posterior pituitary
AP.w: Two steps: large volumes of dilute urine with normal glucose is diabetes insipidus, a deficiency of ADH, and ADH is released from the posterior pituitary.

n.0: Aldosterone is made by the adrenal cortex, not the medulla, and diabetes insipidus is a lack of ADH.
n.1: Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus with high blood glucose, but this patient's glucose is normal.
n.2: The hormone is right, but ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.

AP.q: A few hours after death, the skeletal muscles of the body become stiff and rigid. Which explanation of this rigor mortis is correct?
o: Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Excess acetylcholine keeps restimulating the fibers
Without ATP, myosin heads cannot attach to actin
Without calcium, troponin keeps tropomyosin in place
AP.w: Step 1: after death, ATP production stops. Step 2: ATP must bind a myosin head to release it from actin, so the cross-bridges stay locked and the muscles remain rigid.

n.1: Acetylcholine release requires living motor neurons and is cleared by acetylcholinesterase; the stiffness comes from the lack of ATP.
n.2: If myosin could not attach, the muscles would stay limp; the problem is that attached heads cannot let go.
n.3: Tropomyosin blocking actin would prevent cross-bridges and keep muscle relaxed, not rigid.

AP.q: At the target organs they control, the two autonomic divisions mainly release different neurotransmitters. Which pair lists the main parasympathetic neurotransmitter first and the main sympathetic neurotransmitter second?
AP.w: Parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine at their target organs. The main sympathetic effector neurotransmitter is norepinephrine.

n.1: Acetylcholine is the parasympathetic transmitter; the sympathetic division mainly releases norepinephrine at its targets.
n.2: Epinephrine is mainly a hormone released into the blood by the adrenal medulla; sympathetic nerve endings mainly release norepinephrine.
n.3: This reverses the two divisions: acetylcholine is parasympathetic and norepinephrine is sympathetic.

AP.q: Which vitamin is fat-soluble and is also made in part by bacteria living in the large intestine?
AP.w: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and are absorbed with dietary fat. Bacteria in the large intestine make vitamin K (and some B vitamins), so vitamin K meets both conditions.

n.0: Vitamin D is fat-soluble, but its precursor is made in the skin with UVB light, not by gut bacteria.
n.2: Vitamin C is water-soluble and comes from the diet; intestinal bacteria do not supply it.
n.3: Colon bacteria do make some B vitamins, but vitamin B12 is water-soluble, not fat-soluble.

AP.q: Which set gives the correct number of separate vertebrae in each region of a typical adult's vertebral column, listed as cervical, thoracic, lumbar?
AP.w: An adult has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic (one for each pair of ribs) and 5 lumbar vertebrae, plus the fused sacrum and coccyx: 26 bones in all.

n.0: This swaps the cervical and lumbar counts; the neck has 7 cervical vertebrae.
n.1: This swaps the cervical and thoracic counts; there are 12 thoracic vertebrae to match the 12 pairs of ribs.
n.2: This swaps the thoracic and lumbar counts; there are 5 large lumbar vertebrae.

AP.q: Nervous tissue contains two main categories of cells: neurons and neuroglia. Which statement correctly describes the role of neuroglia?
o: They relay impulses between sensory and motor neurons in the CNS
They carry impulses from receptors toward the brain and spinal cord
They support, insulate and protect neurons but do not conduct impulses
They carry commands from the CNS out to muscles and glands
AP.w: Neuroglia (glial cells) such as astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells support, nourish, insulate (myelin) and protect neurons. Conducting impulses is the job of the neurons themselves.

n.0: Relaying impulses between sensory and motor neurons is the role of interneurons, which are neurons.
n.1: Carrying impulses toward the CNS is the role of sensory (afferent) neurons.
n.3: Carrying commands from the CNS to effectors is the role of motor (efferent) neurons.

AP.q: A patient has lost weight without dieting, feels hot in cool rooms, has a rapid heart rate and has bulging eyes. Excess secretion of which hormones best explains these findings?
o: T3 and T4 from the thyroid gland
Growth hormone from the anterior pituitary
AP.w: T3 and T4 raise metabolic rate and heat production. Excess, as in Graves' disease, causes weight loss, heat intolerance, a fast heart rate and bulging eyes (exophthalmos).

n.1: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium; it does not raise metabolic rate or heat production.
n.2: Excess cortisol causes Cushing's syndrome; heat intolerance, weight loss and bulging eyes point to excess thyroid hormone.
n.3: Excess growth hormone causes gigantism or acromegaly, not this picture of a raised metabolic rate.

AP.q: Serous membranes reduce friction around organs in the ventral cavity. Which layer adheres directly to the outer surface of each lung?
AP.w: Serous membranes have a parietal layer lining the cavity wall and a visceral layer covering the organ. The pleura surrounds the lungs, so the layer on the lung surface is the visceral pleura.

n.1: The parietal peritoneum lines the wall of the abdominopelvic cavity.
n.2: The parietal pleura lines the wall of the thoracic cavity, not the lung surface.
n.3: The visceral pericardium covers the heart, not the lungs.

AP.q: In a classroom demonstration, a chicken bone is soaked in vinegar until its mineral salts dissolve. The bone keeps its shape but can now be bent easily. Which matrix component remains and gives this flexibility?
AP.w: Bone matrix is about one-third organic, mostly collagen (flexibility and tensile strength), and two-thirds inorganic calcium phosphate as hydroxyapatite (hardness). Acid dissolves the mineral and leaves the collagen framework, so the bone bends.

n.1: Osteocytes maintain the matrix but are cells, not the fibrous part of the matrix that resists bending forces.
n.2: Elastin gives stretch and recoil in skin and elastic cartilage; the organic fiber of bone matrix is collagen.
n.3: Hydroxyapatite gives bone its hardness and is the part the acid dissolves; once it is gone the bone loses rigidity.

AP.q: After several axillary lymph nodes are removed during breast cancer surgery, a patient develops lasting swelling of the arm on that side. Which lymphatic function best explains the swelling?
o: Filtering blood and removing worn-out red blood cells
Returning excess interstitial fluid to the blood
Absorbing dietary fats through lacteals in the villi
Filtering lymph to trap microbes before it reaches the blood
AP.w: Lymphatic vessels collect excess interstitial fluid (lymph) and return it to the blood. Removing the axillary nodes disrupts drainage from the arm, so fluid builds up in the tissues.

n.0: Filtering blood and removing old red blood cells is a function of the spleen, not the axillary lymph nodes.
n.2: Lacteals absorb fats in the intestinal villi; they do not drain the arm.
n.3: The nodes do filter lymph, but losing that filter would raise infection risk; the swelling comes from fluid that is no longer drained.

AP.q: A fasting patient's urine test is positive for glucose. In a healthy kidney, where is filtered glucose reabsorbed, and what condition does this finding most suggest?
AP.w: Step 1: the PCT normally reabsorbs all filtered glucose, so urine contains none. Step 2: glucose in the urine (glycosuria) means blood glucose is so high that the PCT is overwhelmed, which suggests diabetes mellitus.

n.0: Diabetes mellitus is the right condition, but glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, not the collecting duct.
n.1: Glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT, and diabetes insipidus causes large volumes of dilute urine, not glucose in urine.
n.2: The PCT is the right site, but diabetes insipidus is an ADH problem causing dilute urine, not glucose in urine.

AP.q: A vessel carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Which statement about this vessel is correct?
o: It is an artery, and its blood is low in oxygen
It is a vein, and its blood is rich in oxygen
It is a vein, and its blood is low in oxygen
It is an artery, and its blood is rich in oxygen
AP.w: Arteries are defined by direction: they carry blood away from the heart, whatever its oxygen content. The pulmonary arteries carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs before gas exchange, so they are arteries carrying oxygen-poor blood.

n.1: A vessel carrying blood away from the heart is an artery, and blood on its way to the lungs is oxygen-poor.
n.2: Low oxygen does not make a vessel a vein; vessels are named by direction, and this one carries blood away from the heart.
n.3: It is an artery, but blood leaving the right ventricle has returned from the body and has not yet picked up oxygen in the lungs.

AP.q: A patient's chart notes a rash in the popliteal region and on the plantar surface of the same leg. Which two areas are affected?
o: The front of the thigh and the sole of the foot
The front of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the sole of the foot
The back of the knee and the top of the foot
AP.w: Two regional terms: popliteal means the back of the knee, and plantar means the sole of the foot.

n.0: The front of the thigh is part of the femoral region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.1: The front of the knee is the patellar region; popliteal is the back of the knee.
n.3: Popliteal is right, but plantar is the sole, not the top of the foot.

AP.q: In an experiment, the receptors that monitor blood pressure in an animal are prevented from sending signals to the brain. Which outcome is most likely?
o: Blood pressure would stay at its set point, because no corrections occur
The effectors would amplify each change until an end event occurred
Changes would go undetected, so blood pressure would vary more widely
The control center would switch the loop over to positive feedback
AP.w: Without receptor input, the control center cannot detect changes from the set point, so it cannot trigger corrective responses. Blood pressure would drift more widely than normal.

n.0: Corrections are what hold a variable near its set point; without them the variable drifts.
n.1: Amplification is a feature of positive feedback loops; losing receptors removes the signal that starts any correction.
n.3: Loss of receptor input does not turn a negative feedback loop into a positive one; the loop simply stops correcting.

AP.q: During quiet, restful breathing, which muscles contract to enlarge the thoracic cavity so that air flows into the lungs?
AP.w: In quiet inspiration the diaphragm (the main muscle of inspiration) contracts and flattens while the external intercostals lift the ribs. Both enlarge the thoracic cavity, pressure in the lungs falls and air flows in. Quiet expiration is mostly passive recoil; the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles act in forced expiration.

n.0: The external intercostals do help, but the rectus abdominis flexes the trunk and assists forced expiration, and the diaphragm is missing.
n.1: The internal intercostals and abdominal muscles such as the rectus abdominis are muscles of forced expiration, not inspiration.
n.3: The diaphragm is right, but the internal intercostals pull the ribs down during forced expiration; they do not act in quiet inspiration.

AP.q: In anatomical position, which choice correctly describes both the forearm bones and the leg bones?
o: Radius lateral to ulna; tibia medial to fibula
Radius medial to ulna; tibia medial to fibula
Radius lateral to ulna; tibia lateral to fibula
Radius medial to ulna; tibia lateral to fibula
AP.w: In anatomical position the palms face forward, so the radius (thumb side) is lateral to the ulna. In the leg, the large weight-bearing tibia is on the medial (big-toe) side and the slender fibula is lateral.

n.1: The tibia is correctly medial, but with the palms forward the radius lies on the thumb side, lateral to the ulna.
n.2: The radius is correctly lateral, but the tibia lies on the big-toe side, medial to the fibula.
n.3: Both halves are reversed: the radius is lateral to the ulna and the tibia is medial to the fibula.

AP.q: A basic spirometer measures the air a person breathes in and out through a mouthpiece. Which lung volume cannot be measured directly with this device?
AP.w: Residual volume is the air that remains in the lungs after the most forceful exhalation; because it is never breathed out, a simple spirometer cannot record it.

n.0: Inspiratory reserve volume is extra air inhaled beyond a normal breath and is measured by spirometry.
n.2: Vital capacity is the total that can be exhaled after a maximal breath, so it is measured directly.
n.3: Expiratory reserve volume is the extra air forced out after a normal exhalation, so the spirometer records it.

AP.q: A spinal cord injury high in the neck damages the nerve that supplies the main muscle of quiet breathing. Which nerve is it?
AP.w: The phrenic nerve, which arises from the cervical spinal cord, supplies the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing.

n.0: The vagus nerve (CN X) carries parasympathetic fibers to thoracic and abdominal organs; it does not drive the diaphragm.
n.1: The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies neck and shoulder muscles such as the trapezius.
n.2: Intercostal nerves supply the intercostal muscles, which assist breathing but are not the main muscle.

AP.q: Stretch receptors in the bladder wall signal that the bladder is full. The signal travels to the spinal cord, and the reply makes the smooth muscle of the bladder wall contract. Which fibers carried the incoming and outgoing signals?
o: Afferent fibers in; somatic motor fibers out
Afferent fibers in; sympathetic fibers out
Afferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
Efferent fibers in; parasympathetic fibers out
AP.w: Two steps: incoming sensory signals travel on afferent fibers, and contraction of the bladder's smooth muscle to promote urination is a parasympathetic (autonomic motor) effect.

n.0: Somatic motor fibers control skeletal muscle; the bladder wall is smooth muscle under autonomic control.
n.1: The sympathetic division slows urination; the parasympathetic division contracts the bladder wall.
n.3: Signals entering the CNS travel on afferent fibers; efferent fibers carry commands out.

AP.q: A night-shift nurse finds that her normal sleep-wake rhythm is disrupted. Which gland and hormone normally regulate this rhythm, with secretion rising in darkness?
AP.w: The pineal gland secretes melatonin, which rises in darkness and regulates the sleep-wake (circadian) rhythm.

n.0: The pineal gland is right, but cortisol is made by the adrenal cortex.
n.1: The anterior pituitary makes ACTH, not cortisol (adrenal cortex) or melatonin (pineal gland).
n.3: Melatonin comes from the pineal gland, not the anterior pituitary.

AP.q: Starting from anatomical position, a patient turns the forearm so that the palm faces backward, with the radius crossing over the ulna. What is this movement called?
AP.w: Pronation turns the palm to face posteriorly (or downward) as the radius crosses over the ulna. Supination is the reverse, returning the palm to face anteriorly as in anatomical position.

n.0: Circumduction is a cone-shaped movement of a limb, as at the shoulder or hip.
n.1: Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward; it is a foot movement.
n.2: Supination turns the palm forward or upward; in anatomical position the forearm is already supinated.

AP.q: A hiker rounds a bend and nearly steps on a rattlesnake. Which combination of changes would his autonomic nervous system most likely produce in the next few seconds?
o: Faster heart rate, dilated pupils and increased digestion
Faster heart rate, constricted pupils and slowed digestion
Slower heart rate, dilated pupils and increased digestion
Faster heart rate, dilated pupils and slowed digestion
AP.w: A sudden threat triggers the sympathetic (fight or flight) division, which increases the heart rate, dilates the pupils and slows digestion at the same time.

n.0: Sympathetic stimulation slows digestion; increased digestion is a parasympathetic (rest and digest) effect.
n.1: Constricted pupils are a parasympathetic effect; sympathetic stimulation dilates them.
n.2: A slower heart rate and increased digestion are parasympathetic effects; the sympathetic response speeds the heart and slows digestion.

AP.q: Which vessel in the umbilical cord carries oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus?
AP.w: The umbilical cord normally holds one umbilical vein, which brings oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus, and two umbilical arteries, which carry deoxygenated blood and wastes back to the placenta.

n.0: A normal cord has only one umbilical vein, not two.
n.1: A normal cord has two umbilical arteries, and they carry deoxygenated blood, not oxygen-rich blood.
n.3: The two umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus to the placenta.

AP.q: A clinic records an adult's blood pressure as 118/76 mmHg. What does the 76 represent?
o: Arterial pressure while the ventricles contract (systolic pressure)
Arterial pressure while the ventricles relax (diastolic pressure)
Arterial pressure while the atria contract at the end of filling
Venous pressure while the ventricles relax and fill with blood
AP.w: Blood pressure is written systolic/diastolic. The lower number (76) is the diastolic pressure in the arteries while the ventricles relax and fill.

n.0: Systolic pressure, during ventricular contraction, is the top number (118).
n.2: Diastolic pressure is the minimum arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation; it is not defined by atrial contraction.
n.3: A blood pressure cuff measures arterial pressure, not venous pressure.

AP.q: Atrial repolarization does not appear as a separate wave on a normal ECG. Why?
o: It occurs during the QRS complex and is hidden by it
It occurs during the T wave and is hidden by it
It occurs after the T wave and is too small to record
It occurs during the P wave and is hidden by it
AP.w: The atria repolarize at about the same time the ventricles depolarize, so the small atrial repolarization signal is masked by the much larger QRS complex.

n.1: The T wave is ventricular repolarization, which happens later, while the atria are already at rest.
n.2: After the T wave the whole heart is at rest; the atria repolarized much earlier.
n.3: The P wave is atrial depolarization; repolarization cannot occur at the same moment.

AP.q: Brush-border enzymes complete the chemical digestion of carbohydrates in the small intestine. Which set lists the end products that are absorbed into the blood?
AP.w: Carbohydrates are absorbed only as monosaccharides: glucose, fructose and galactose. Maltase, sucrase and lactase split the disaccharides to produce them.

n.0: Starch and glycogen are polysaccharides, far too large to be absorbed.
n.2: Glycerol and fatty acids come from fat digestion, not carbohydrate digestion.
n.3: Maltose, sucrose and lactose are disaccharides that brush-border enzymes still have to split before absorption.

AP.q: A slide of tissue from a gland duct shows a single layer of cells that are about as tall as they are wide, each resting on the basement membrane. Which name fits this tissue?
AP.w: Epithelium is named by layers and cell shape. One layer is "simple," and cells about as tall as they are wide are "cuboidal," giving simple cuboidal epithelium.

n.0: Pseudostratified epithelium has tall cells with nuclei at different heights that look layered; these cells are cube-shaped.
n.2: Columnar cells are taller than they are wide; these cells are about equal in height and width.
n.3: "Stratified" means two or more layers; the sample has one layer.

AP.q: A patient who spends almost no time outdoors develops low blood calcium. Which sequence best describes the skin's normal role in calcium absorption from the intestine?
o: Melanocytes secrete vitamin D3 after UVB exposure; the kidneys then activate it
UVB converts a cholesterol derivative directly into active calcitriol in skin
Sebaceous glands secrete vitamin D3 in sebum; the liver then activates it
UVB makes vitamin D3 from a cholesterol derivative; liver and kidneys activate it
AP.w: Step 1: in the skin, UVB converts a cholesterol derivative to vitamin D3, an inactive precursor. Step 2: the liver and kidneys convert it to active calcitriol, which increases calcium absorption from the gut. Little sun means little D3 and poorer Ca²⁺ absorption.

n.0: Melanocytes make melanin, which absorbs UV; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative in the skin, and the liver also takes part in activation.
n.1: The skin makes only the precursor; activation to calcitriol takes place in the liver and kidneys.
n.2: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum to lubricate skin; vitamin D3 forms from a cholesterol derivative, and the kidneys also take part in activation.

BI.q: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA shows that 22% of its bases are thymine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
BI.w: Step 1: A = T, so A is also 22%, and A + T = 44%. Step 2: G + C = 100% - 44% = 56%. Step 3: G = C, so G = 56% / 2 = 28%.

n.1: 22% is the share of thymine (and of adenine); guanine pairs with cytosine, not with thymine.
n.2: 56% is guanine and cytosine together; guanine is half of that total.
n.3: 78% subtracts thymine alone from 100%; adenine (also 22%) must be subtracted too, and the rest halved.

BI.q: In sickle cell anemia, a single base substitution in the beta-globin gene causes valine to replace glutamic acid in the hemoglobin chain. Which type of mutation is this?
BI.w: A missense mutation is a point substitution that changes one amino acid to a different one, as in sickle cell (glutamic acid to valine).

n.0: A nonsense mutation creates a stop codon and shortens the protein; here the chain is full length with one amino acid changed.
n.1: A frameshift results from inserting or deleting bases, not from substituting one base.
n.3: A silent mutation leaves the amino acid unchanged; here the amino acid changes.

BI.q: During meiosis I, both copies of chromosome 21 end up in one egg, which a normal sperm then fertilizes. What will the zygote most likely have?
o: 45 chromosomes, the pattern seen in Turner syndrome
47 chromosomes, with an XXY set of sex chromosomes
45 chromosomes, with one copy of chromosome 21
47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21
BI.w: Step 1: nondisjunction gives the egg 24 chromosomes, including two copies of chromosome 21. Step 2: adding a normal sperm's 23 gives 47, with three copies of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21, Down syndrome).

n.0: Turner syndrome (45,X) is a missing sex chromosome. This egg has an extra chromosome, so the total rises above 46.
n.1: XXY (Klinefelter syndrome) involves the sex chromosomes, but the nondisjunction here involved chromosome 21.
n.2: A zygote with one chromosome 21 would come from an egg that received no copy. Here the egg received both copies.

BI.q: A patient with lactose intolerance makes too little lactase. When lactase does digest lactose, which two monosaccharides are released?
BI.w: Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose. Lactase hydrolyzes it into those two monosaccharides.

n.1: Galactose + fructose is not one of the common dietary disaccharides.
n.2: Glucose + glucose make maltose.
n.3: Glucose + fructose make sucrose (table sugar).

BI.q: The coding region of an mRNA, from the start codon AUG through the stop codon, is 450 nucleotides long. How many amino acids will the resulting polypeptide contain?
BI.w: Step 1: each codon is 3 nucleotides, so 450 / 3 = 150 codons. Step 2: the last codon is a stop codon, which codes for no amino acid, so 150 - 1 = 149 amino acids.

n.0: 450 counts one nucleotide per amino acid; each amino acid needs a three-base codon.
n.2: 225 divides by 2, but a codon is three bases long, not two.
n.3: 150 is the number of codons; the final stop codon codes for no amino acid.

BI.q: Bread dough rises when yeast cells, deprived of oxygen inside the dough, break down sugar and release a gas. Which process is responsible, and what does it produce?
o: Aerobic respiration, producing water and oxygen gas
Lactic acid fermentation, producing lactic acid and CO₂
Photosynthesis, producing glucose and oxygen gas
Alcoholic fermentation, producing ethanol and CO₂
BI.w: Without oxygen, yeast carry out alcoholic fermentation: glycolysis followed by conversion of pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide. The CO₂ bubbles make the dough rise.

n.0: The yeast lack oxygen, and aerobic respiration consumes oxygen rather than producing it.
n.1: Lactic acid fermentation occurs in human muscle and releases no CO₂, so it would not raise dough.
n.2: Yeast are fungi and cannot photosynthesize; photosynthesis also uses CO₂ rather than releasing it.

BI.q: When a DNA sample is gently heated, its two strands separate, yet each strand's sugar-phosphate backbone stays intact. Which bonds were broken?
BI.w: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (2 for A-T, 3 for G-C). The backbone is held by strong covalent phosphodiester bonds, which stay intact.

n.0: Glycosidic bonds join sugars in carbohydrates; DNA strands are not held together this way.
n.1: Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins, not nucleotides.
n.3: Phosphodiester bonds form the backbone, which the stem says stayed intact.
