BI.q: In a lab, red blood cells are placed in a 5% sodium chloride solution, which is hypertonic to the cells. What will most likely happen to the cells?
o: There is no net water movement, so the cells keep their shape.
Water enters the cells, which swell and undergo hemolysis.
Sodium enters the cells, which swell as solute builds up.
Water leaves the cells, which shrink and undergo crenation.
BI.w: A hypertonic solution has more solute outside the cell, so water leaves by osmosis and the red blood cells shrink (crenation).

n.0: No net water movement describes an isotonic solution such as 0.9% NaCl, not a 5% solution.
n.1: Swelling and hemolysis happen in a hypotonic solution, where water moves into the cell.
n.2: Osmosis is the movement of water, not solute. The cells lose water and shrink.

BI.q: A woman who is a carrier of hemophilia A (XHXh) and a man without hemophilia (XHY) plan a family. What percentage of their sons are expected to have hemophilia?
BI.w: Sons get the Y from the father and one X from the mother. Half of the mother's eggs carry Xh, so 1/2 = 50% of sons (XhY) are expected to have hemophilia.

n.1: 100% assumes every son of a carrier is affected; the mother passes Xh to only half of her sons.
n.2: 0% assumes sons inherit X-linked alleles from the father; sons get their X from the mother.
n.3: 25% is the share of all children expected to be affected sons; among sons alone it is half.

BI.q: Lactase breaks down lactose but has no effect on sucrose. What best explains this specificity?
o: Lactase is used up by lactose before sucrose.
Sucrose does not fit lactase's active site.
BI.w: An enzyme's active site matches the shape of its own substrate (lock-and-key, induced fit). Sucrose does not fit lactase's active site, so it is not broken down.

n.0: Sucrose does not unfold the enzyme; it simply does not bind.
n.1: Enzymes are not consumed by the reactions they catalyze.
n.3: Enzymes lower activation energy; a substrate does not raise it.

BI.q: Why are viruses not classified in any of the three domains of life (Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya)?
o: They do not change over generations.
They are not made of cells.
BI.w: The domains classify cellular life. Viruses are not made of cells: they are genetic material in a protein coat and reproduce inside host cells.

n.0: Viruses do change over generations; their genes mutate and the populations evolve.
n.2: Viruses do carry genetic material (DNA or RNA); that is how they direct host cells to make new viruses.
n.3: Prokaryotes are cells without a nucleus; viruses are not cells at all.

BI.q: Cells in a tumor keep dividing even when they are crowded and their DNA is damaged. Which part of cell cycle control has most likely failed?
BI.w: Checkpoints normally stop the cycle when DNA is damaged or conditions are wrong. When they fail, cells divide uncontrollably, which leads to cancer.

n.1: Crossing over occurs in meiosis, not in the mitotic divisions of tumor cells.
n.2: S phase copies DNA; uncontrolled division comes from failed control, not from replication itself.
n.3: Cytokinesis is the final split of the cytoplasm; it does not decide whether a cell divides.

BI.q: A toxin blocks the electron transport chain in a patient's cells. Which change in those cells would be expected?
o: Glucose is broken down directly into CO₂ in the cytoplasm.
Oxygen use rises, as more is needed to accept electrons.
ATP output holds steady, as the Krebs cycle makes up the loss.
ATP output drops, and cells shift to lactic acid fermentation.
BI.w: Step 1: the electron transport chain makes most of the cell's ATP, so blocking it causes a sharp fall in ATP. Step 2: cells fall back on glycolysis, which needs no oxygen, regenerating its needs by lactic acid fermentation.

n.0: CO₂ is released in the mitochondria (pyruvate oxidation and Krebs cycle), not from glucose in the cytoplasm.
n.1: Oxygen is used only as the final electron acceptor of the chain, so a blocked chain uses less oxygen, not more.
n.2: The Krebs cycle makes only a little ATP and stalls when the chain stops regenerating NAD+ and FAD, so it cannot replace the chain's output.

BI.q: Towns beside a large lake have milder temperature swings than towns farther inland. Which property of water best explains this?
BI.w: Water's high specific heat lets it absorb and release large amounts of heat with little change in its own temperature, which moderates the nearby climate.

n.0: Floating ice insulates the water below but does not explain milder air temperatures year-round.
n.2: Cohesion produces surface tension; it does not store heat.
n.3: Low specific heat would make the lake heat and cool quickly, worsening the swings.

BI.q: A student sets up a model in which a dye diffuses across a membrane from a concentrated solution into a dilute one. Which change would increase the rate of diffusion?
o: Using a dye that has much larger molecules
Making the membrane twice as thick as before
Raising the temperature of the solutions
BI.w: Diffusion is faster at higher temperature, with a steeper concentration gradient, smaller molecules, greater surface area and a shorter distance.

n.0: Larger molecules diffuse more slowly than smaller ones.
n.1: A thicker membrane increases the distance, which slows diffusion.
n.2: Diluting the concentrated side makes the gradient less steep, which slows diffusion.

BI.q: A weightlifter builds large muscles over ten years of training. According to modern evolutionary theory, how will this affect his future children?
o: Their muscles will be larger from birth.
They will inherit part of his extra muscle.
It will have no effect on the traits they inherit.
They will build muscle faster when they train.
BI.w: Traits acquired during life, such as trained muscles, do not change the DNA in sperm, so they are not inherited (Lamarck's idea was rejected).

n.0: Larger muscles at birth would require inherited acquired traits, which do not occur.
n.1: Muscle gained by training changes body tissue, not the genes in sperm, so none of it is inherited.
n.3: His training does not alter the alleles he passes on, so it does not speed his children's muscle growth.

BI.q: When an egg white is cooked, the protein albumin turns from clear to opaque white and does not return to its original form on cooling. What happened?
o: Its amino acid sequence was rearranged.
It was denatured and lost its folded shape.
It gained new amino acids from the heat.
Its peptide bonds broke into free amino acids.
BI.w: Heat denatures proteins: it disrupts the bonds that hold the folded shape, so the protein unfolds and loses its function. The peptide bonds and sequence stay intact.

n.0: The primary sequence is unchanged by denaturation; only the folding is lost.
n.2: Heating adds no amino acids; the same chain unfolds.
n.3: Denaturation leaves peptide bonds intact; breaking them would require hydrolysis.

BI.q: Most leaves look green in sunlight. Which statement best explains this in terms of how chlorophyll interacts with light?
o: It absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green.
It absorbs mostly green light and reflects red and blue.
It absorbs mostly green light and turns it into glucose.
It absorbs ultraviolet light and gives it off as green.
BI.w: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly red and blue wavelengths for photosynthesis and reflects green, which is the color we see.

n.1: This is reversed. A pigment looks the color it reflects, so green is the color chlorophyll absorbs least.
n.2: Green light is mostly reflected, so it contributes little energy to making glucose.
n.3: Leaves are green because of reflected green light, not because chlorophyll converts ultraviolet light into green.

BI.q: Pure water has a pH of 7. Which statement explains this neutral pH?
o: Its polar charges cancel out any H+ ions.
It ionizes into more OH- than H+ ions.
It does not ionize, so no ions are present.
It ionizes slightly into equal H+ and OH-.
BI.w: A few water molecules split into H+ (as H3O+) and OH-. In pure water the two are equal, so the solution is neutral, pH 7.

n.0: Partial charges on molecules do not remove H+ ions; neutrality comes from equal H+ and OH-.
n.1: More OH- than H+ would make the solution basic, above pH 7.
n.2: Water does ionize slightly; that small amount of H+ and OH- gives pH 7.

BI.q: A man with red-green color blindness, an X-linked recessive trait, has children with a woman who carries no color-blindness allele. Which outcome is expected?
o: Half of the sons are color-blind and half of the daughters are carriers.
All of the daughters are carriers and none of the sons are color-blind.
Half of the daughters are color-blind and none of the sons are affected.
All of the sons are color-blind and none of the daughters are carriers.
BI.w: Step 1: the father passes his X (with the allele) to every daughter and his Y to every son. Step 2: daughters get a normal X from the mother, so all are carriers; sons get the mother's normal X, so none are affected.

n.0: This is the pattern for a carrier mother and a normal father, not an affected father and a noncarrier mother.
n.2: Each daughter gets a normal X from her mother, which masks the recessive allele, so she is a carrier, not affected.
n.3: Sons receive the father's Y, not his X, so they cannot inherit his X-linked allele.

BI.q: A nursing student is matching membrane processes to examples for a study sheet. Which pairing is correct?
o: Facilitated diffusion: the pump that moves Na⁺ and K⁺ ions
Active transport: oxygen moving into a red blood cell
Exocytosis: a neuron releasing neurotransmitter from vesicles
Phagocytosis: a cell taking in droplets of extracellular fluid
BI.w: Exocytosis releases material from the cell when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, as in neurotransmitter, hormone and enzyme secretion.

n.0: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to move ions against their gradients, which is active transport.
n.1: Oxygen enters red blood cells by simple diffusion down its gradient, with no ATP.
n.3: Taking in fluid droplets is pinocytosis (cell drinking). Phagocytosis engulfs solid particles such as bacteria.

BI.q: A patient receives a bone marrow transplant so that the marrow can again produce red cells, white cells and platelets. Which donated cells make this possible?
o: Mature white blood cells that change their type
Embryonic stem cells that can form any cell
Mature red blood cells that divide by mitosis
Adult stem cells that form several blood cells
BI.w: Bone marrow holds adult (blood-forming) stem cells: unspecialized cells that divide and differentiate into red cells, white cells and platelets. Adult stem cells form a more limited range of cell types than embryonic stem cells.

n.0: Mature white blood cells are already specialized; they do not convert into red cells or platelets.
n.1: Embryonic stem cells come from an early embryo, not from an adult donor's bone marrow.
n.2: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and cannot divide.

BI.q: In the first minutes of intense exercise, which class of macromolecule do muscle cells use as their main quick source of energy?
BI.w: Carbohydrates (glucose and stored glycogen) are the main quick energy source. Lipids store the most energy per gram but are long-term fuel.

n.0: Nucleic acids carry genetic information, not fuel.
n.1: Triglycerides hold more energy per gram but are long-term storage, released more slowly.
n.3: Myosin is a contractile protein; proteins are not the preferred fuel.

BI.q: On a bright, warm afternoon, a greenhouse plant's rate of photosynthesis stops rising as light increases. Which change would most likely raise the rate?
o: Green light in place of white light
Less water given to the roots
More oxygen in the greenhouse air
More carbon dioxide in the air
BI.w: When light is no longer limiting, another factor is: raising CO2 gives the Calvin cycle more raw material to fix, so the rate rises.

n.0: Chlorophyll reflects most green light, so green light would lower the rate.
n.1: Water is a raw material; reducing it would slow photosynthesis.
n.2: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis; adding it does not speed the process.

BI.q: In a population of white-tailed deer, which individual has the highest evolutionary fitness?
o: The oldest doe, which raised one fawn
The fastest buck, which outran every predator
The largest buck, which wins the most fights
A doe that raised five fawns that later bred
BI.w: Fitness is reproductive success: the number of surviving, fertile offspring an individual leaves. The doe with five breeding fawns passes on the most alleles.

n.0: A long life with one fawn passes on fewer alleles than five fawns that breed.
n.1: Escaping predators helps survival, but fitness is measured in offspring, not speed.
n.2: Size and strength are not fitness unless they produce more surviving offspring.

BI.q: Snapdragon color shows incomplete dominance: red (RR), pink (RW), white (WW). Two pink plants are crossed and produce 240 seedlings. How many are expected to have pink flowers?
BI.w: RW x RW gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW, so 2/4 = 1/2 are pink. 240 x 1/2 = 120.

n.0: 240 assumes pink plants breed true; RW x RW also gives red and white offspring.
n.1: 60 is the size of the red class (or of the white class), each 1/4 of the seedlings.
n.2: 180 uses the 3:1 ratio of complete dominance; here the heterozygotes form a separate pink class.

BI.q: Which observation provides the strongest support for the hypothesis that mitochondria descended from prokaryotes engulfed by an ancestral cell?
o: They have their own circular DNA and a double membrane.
They produce most of the ATP made by the cell.
They are found in plant cells as well as animal cells.
They are more numerous in muscle cells than in skin cells.
BI.w: Endosymbiotic theory is supported by features mitochondria share with bacteria: their own circular DNA and ribosomes, a double membrane, and division by binary fission.

n.1: Producing most of the ATP is the function of mitochondria, not evidence of where they came from.
n.2: Being present in plants and animals is true, but it says nothing about a prokaryotic origin.
n.3: Higher numbers in active cells reflect energy demand, not ancestry.

BI.q: A researcher compares the DNA of a bacterium with the DNA of a human white blood cell. Which description fits the bacterial DNA?
o: A single circular chromosome, often with plasmids
Several linear chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope
Linear chromosomes coiled around histone proteins
RNA in place of DNA, packed inside a protein capsid
BI.w: Bacteria usually carry one circular chromosome in the nucleoid region, often with small extra circles of DNA called plasmids.

n.1: Multiple linear chromosomes in a nucleus describe the human (eukaryotic) cell, not the bacterium.
n.2: Histone packaging into chromatin is a eukaryotic feature.
n.3: Some viruses carry RNA inside a capsid. Bacteria are cells and store their genes in DNA.

BI.q: Which pair of organisms are both autotrophs?
o: A fern and a bread yeast
A moss and a green alga
A pine tree and a mushroom
BI.w: Autotrophs make their own food, usually by photosynthesis. Mosses and green algae both contain chlorophyll and photosynthesize.

n.0: The fern is an autotroph, but yeast is a fungus, a heterotroph.
n.1: Grass is an autotroph, but an amoeba is a protist that engulfs food, a heterotroph.
n.3: The pine is an autotroph, but a mushroom is a fungus, a heterotroph that absorbs food.

BI.q: A drug shaped like an enzyme's substrate binds the active site and slows the reaction. Adding much more substrate restores the normal rate. Which type of inhibition is this?
BI.w: A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and competes with the substrate, so raising substrate concentration can overcome it.

n.0: A noncompetitive (allosteric) inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape; extra substrate does not overcome it.
n.2: Denaturation is loss of enzyme shape from heat or extreme pH, not binding of an inhibitor.
n.3: Saturation is the plateau reached when all active sites are busy; it is not inhibition.

CH.q: A sealed bottle of soda fizzes as soon as the cap is removed. Which statement best explains this?
o: The pressure drops, so less CO₂ stays dissolved
Opening warms the soda, so less gas dissolves
The pressure drops, so more CO₂ can dissolve
Air enters and reacts with the dissolved CO₂
CH.w: The bottle is sealed under high CO₂ pressure. Gas solubility rises with pressure (Henry's law), so when the cap comes off and the pressure falls, less CO₂ can stay dissolved and it forms bubbles.

n.1: Removing the cap does not change the soda's temperature; the pressure drop causes the fizzing.
n.2: Lower pressure lowers gas solubility; it does not let more CO₂ dissolve.
n.3: CO₂ does not react with air; it simply comes out of solution.

CH.q: A nucleus releases radiation, but its mass number and atomic number stay exactly the same. Which type of radiation was released?
CH.w: A gamma ray is a high-energy photon with no mass and no charge, so emitting it changes neither the mass number nor the atomic number; the nucleus only loses energy.

n.0: Beta emission keeps the mass number but raises the atomic number by 1.
n.1: Positron emission keeps the mass number but lowers the atomic number by 1.
n.3: Alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

CH.q: Copper is drawn into thin wires for electrical cables and conducts electricity very well. Which type of bonding between copper atoms explains these properties?
o: Metallic bonding, with delocalized electrons moving among cations
Hydrogen bonding, with weak attractions between copper atoms
Covalent bonding, with electron pairs shared between copper atoms
Ionic bonding, with electrons transferred between copper atoms
CH.w: In metallic bonding, metal cations sit in a sea of delocalized electrons. The mobile electrons carry current, and the cations can slide past one another without breaking the bond, which makes metals ductile and malleable.

n.1: Hydrogen bonds need hydrogen bonded to N, O or F; they do not form between copper atoms.
n.2: Localized shared pairs would not let electrons flow freely or let layers slide, so covalent bonding cannot explain conduction and ductility.
n.3: Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal; identical copper atoms do not transfer electrons to one another.

CH.q: What is the mass of 0.200 mol of sodium chloride, NaCl? (Use Na = 23.0, Cl = 35.5.)
CH.w: Molar mass of NaCl = 23.0 + 35.5 = 58.5 g/mol. Mass = moles × molar mass = 0.200 × 58.5 = 11.7 g.

n.0: 117 g moves the decimal point one place: 0.200 × 58.5 is 11.7.
n.1: 58.5 g is the mass of one full mole, not 0.200 mol.
n.3: 293 g divides the molar mass by the moles (58.5 ÷ 0.200 = 292.5); mass = moles × molar mass.

CH.q: In a water molecule, the oxygen atom pulls the shared electrons more strongly than the hydrogen atoms do. Which choice correctly describes the O-H bonds and the water molecule as a whole?
o: Polar covalent bonds in a linear, nonpolar molecule
Polar covalent bonds in a bent, polar molecule
Ionic bonds in a bent molecule with full charges
Nonpolar covalent bonds in a bent, polar molecule
CH.w: Unequal sharing makes each O-H bond polar covalent: oxygen gets a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge. Because the molecule is bent, the bond polarities do not cancel, so water is a polar molecule.

n.0: Water is bent, not linear. A linear shape (as in CO₂) would let the bond polarities cancel.
n.2: Electrons are shared, not fully transferred, between oxygen and hydrogen, so there are partial charges, not full ionic charges.
n.3: Nonpolar bonds involve equal sharing; oxygen's stronger pull makes the O-H bonds polar.

CH.q: A plastic bead has a mass of 12 g and a volume of 15 mL. What happens when it is dropped into water (density 1.0 g/mL), and why?
o: It floats, because its density is 0.08 g/mL
It floats, because its density is 0.8 g/mL
It sinks, because its density is 1.25 g/mL
It sinks, because its density is 1.8 g/mL
CH.w: Step 1: density = mass / volume = 12 g / 15 mL = 0.8 g/mL. Step 2: an object less dense than the fluid it is placed in floats; 0.8 g/mL is less than water's 1.0 g/mL, so the bead floats.

n.0: The bead does float, but 0.08 g/mL is a decimal-place slip; 12 / 15 = 0.8.
n.2: 1.25 g/mL comes from dividing volume by mass (15 / 12). Density is mass divided by volume.
n.3: 1.8 g/mL comes from adding mass and volume before dividing; density is simply 12 / 15.

CH.q: A student mixes two clear, colorless solutions in a test tube. Within seconds, a cloudy yellow solid forms and slowly settles to the bottom. What does this observation most likely indicate?
o: A chemical change, because a precipitate has formed
A physical change, because two liquids were mixed
A physical change, because the solid can be filtered off
A chemical change, because the mixture is now uneven
CH.w: The formation of a precipitate (an insoluble solid) from two solutions is a sign of a chemical change: a new substance with new properties has been produced. Other signs include unexpected gas, color change, light and temperature change.

n.1: Mixing alone can be physical, but here a new solid substance appeared, which signals a reaction.
n.2: Being able to separate the solid by filtration does not make the change physical; the solid is a newly formed substance.
n.3: The change is chemical, but the reason is the new substance; a heterogeneous mixture can also form by purely physical mixing.

CH.q: Ammonia reacts with water according to NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which substance acts as a Bronsted-Lowry base in the forward reaction, and why?
o: NH₃, because it accepts a proton from water
NH₃, because it donates a proton to water
NH₃, because it contains a hydroxide ion
H₂O, because it accepts a proton from NH₃
CH.w: A Bronsted-Lowry base is a proton (H⁺) acceptor. NH₃ takes an H⁺ from water and becomes NH₄⁺, so NH₃ is the base and water acts as the acid (proton donor).

n.1: Donating a proton is what an acid does. NH₃ gains a proton to become NH₄⁺.
n.2: NH₃ contains no hydroxide ion; it is a base because it accepts a proton, which is the point of the Bronsted-Lowry definition.
n.3: Water loses a proton here (becoming OH⁻), so water is the acid, not the base.

CH.q: Boron has two stable isotopes, boron-10 and boron-11, and its average atomic mass is 10.8 amu. What does this average show?
o: Boron-10 is the more abundant of the two isotopes
Boron-11 is the more abundant of the two isotopes
The two isotopes occur in about equal amounts
Most boron atoms have a mass of exactly 10.8 amu
CH.w: A weighted average lies closer to the mass of the more abundant isotope. 10.8 is much closer to 11 than to 10, so boron-11 makes up most natural boron.

n.0: If boron-10 were more common, the average would sit closer to 10, not at 10.8.
n.2: Equal amounts would give an average of about 10.5, halfway between the two masses.
n.3: No single boron atom has a mass of 10.8; each atom is boron-10 or boron-11, and 10.8 is their weighted average.

CH.q: An atom of iron-56 has an atomic number of 26. How many neutrons are in the nucleus of this atom?
CH.w: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 56 - 26 = 30.

n.0: 56 is the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons together.
n.1: 82 adds the mass number and the atomic number; neutrons come from subtracting them.
n.2: 26 is the number of protons (the atomic number), not the number of neutrons.

CH.q: A lab report lists three elements measured in a patient's blood tests by their symbols: K, Na and Fe. Which names match these symbols, in the same order?
CH.w: Several symbols come from Latin names: K is potassium (kalium), Na is sodium (natrium) and Fe is iron (ferrum).

n.0: Krypton's symbol is Kr. K is potassium.
n.1: Nitrogen's symbol is N. Na is sodium.
n.3: Calcium's symbol is Ca. K is potassium.

CH.q: A chemist adds a catalyst to a reaction mixture that has already reached equilibrium. What happens to the equilibrium amounts of reactants and products?
o: They stay the same, because both rates rise equally
They shift toward more products, as the forward rate rises
They shift toward more reactants, as the reverse rate rises
They change as the catalyst is gradually used up
CH.w: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse reactions equally, so both rates increase by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached faster, but the equilibrium amounts do not change, and the catalyst is not consumed.

n.1: The forward rate does rise, but the reverse rate rises equally, so there is no net shift toward products.
n.2: The reverse rate rises, but by the same factor as the forward rate, so there is no shift toward reactants.
n.3: A catalyst is not consumed by the reaction; it is recovered unchanged at the end.

CH.q: Ethanol burns in a camp stove: C₂H₅OH + 3 O₂ → 2 CO₂ + 3 H₂O. Which type of reaction is this?
CH.w: Combustion: a fuel containing carbon and hydrogen reacts with O₂ to produce CO₂ and H₂O and release energy.

n.1: Decomposition starts from one reactant; this reaction has two, including O₂.
n.2: Synthesis gives a single product; this reaction gives two.
n.3: Double replacement swaps ions between two compounds; here a fuel reacts with oxygen gas.

CH.q: Neon is used in lighted signs partly because it does not react with the glass tube or the metal electrodes. What best explains neon's very low chemical reactivity?
o: Its outer shell is already full with 8 electrons
Its 8 valence electrons are easily shared in bonds
Its ionization energy is the lowest in period 2
Its large atomic radius keeps other atoms away
CH.w: Neon is a noble gas (group 18). Its outer shell is full (2, 8), so it has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, which makes it very unreactive.

n.1: A full octet is stable; neon does not share its valence electrons to form bonds.
n.2: Neon has the highest, not the lowest, ionization energy in period 2; a low ionization energy (as in lithium) makes an element react readily.
n.3: Size does not explain it: argon and krypton are larger noble gases and are also unreactive, because they too have a full outer shell.

CH.q: Which of these equations represents a synthesis reaction?
CH.w: In synthesis (A + B → AB) two or more reactants combine into one product: calcium oxide and water form calcium hydroxide.

n.1: One compound breaking into simpler substances is decomposition.
n.2: A free element (Mg) replacing hydrogen in a compound is single replacement.
n.3: An acid and a base forming a salt and water is neutralization, with two products.

CH.q: An athletic trainer squeezes an instant cold pack, and it turns cold as ammonium nitrate dissolves in water. How is this process classified?
o: Endothermic, releasing heat to the skin
Endothermic, absorbing heat from the skin
Exothermic, releasing heat to the skin
Exothermic, absorbing heat from the skin
CH.w: The pack feels cold because the dissolving process absorbs energy from its surroundings, including the skin. A process that absorbs heat is endothermic (delta H positive).

n.0: Endothermic is correct, but an endothermic process takes in heat; releasing heat would warm the skin.
n.2: An exothermic process releases heat and would feel warm, like a hand warmer.
n.3: Absorbing heat is correct, but a process that absorbs heat is endothermic, not exothermic.

CH.q: How many oxygen atoms are represented by 2 Al₂(SO₄)₃?
CH.w: One Al₂(SO₄)₃ has 3 sulfate groups × 4 O = 12 O. The coefficient 2 doubles it: 2 × 12 = 24 oxygen atoms.

n.0: 12 is the oxygen count in one formula unit; the coefficient 2 doubles it.
n.1: 9 adds the numbers (2 + 3 + 4) instead of multiplying them.
n.3: 8 multiplies 2 × 4 and skips the subscript 3 outside the parentheses.

CH.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂?
CH.w: Hydrogen is +1, so 2(+1) + 2(O) = 0 and each O = −1. Peroxides are the exception to oxygen's usual −2.

n.0: 0 is the oxidation number of oxygen in the free element, O₂.
n.1: −2 is oxygen's usual value, but peroxides are the exception: 2(+1) + 2(−2) would not sum to 0.
n.3: +1 is hydrogen's oxidation number in this compound, not oxygen's.

CH.q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is described as a strong acid, while the acetic acid in vinegar is a weak acid. What does the term 'strong' refer to?
o: How completely the acid ionizes in water
How many hydrogen atoms each molecule holds
How concentrated the acid solution is
How much base is needed to neutralize it
CH.w: Acid strength refers to the degree of ionization: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely in water, while a weak acid such as acetic acid ionizes only partially.

n.1: The number of hydrogen atoms does not set strength; acetic acid (CH₃COOH) has four hydrogens but is weak.
n.2: Concentration is how much acid is dissolved in a volume; a strong acid can be dilute and a weak acid concentrated.
n.3: The amount of base needed depends on the moles of acid present, not on whether the acid is strong or weak.

CH.q: During rusting, 4 Fe + 3 O₂ → 2 Fe₂O₃. What happens to the oxidation number of iron?
o: It falls from +3 to 0; iron is reduced
It rises from 0 to +3; iron is oxidized
It rises from 0 to +3; iron is reduced
It rises from 0 to +2; iron is oxidized
CH.w: Free iron is 0. In Fe₂O₃, 2 Fe + 3(−2) = 0, so each Fe is +3. An increase in oxidation number (loss of electrons) is oxidation.

n.0: Iron starts as the free element (0) and ends in Fe₂O₃ (+3); the change runs upward.
n.2: The numbers are right, but a rising oxidation number means electrons were lost: oxidation.
n.3: +2 is iron's number in FeO; in Fe₂O₃, 2 Fe must balance 3 O at −2, giving +3.

CH.q: Sodium, a reactive metal, combines with chlorine, a nonmetal, to form sodium chloride (NaCl), the main salt in normal saline. Which statement correctly describes the bond in NaCl?
o: Covalent, formed as the two atoms share a pair of electrons
Metallic, formed by a sea of electrons around both atoms
Ionic, formed as sodium transfers an electron to chlorine
Ionic, formed as chlorine transfers an electron to sodium
CH.w: A metal and a nonmetal with a large difference in electronegativity form an ionic bond. Sodium loses its single valence electron to chlorine, producing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that are held together by electrostatic attraction.

n.0: Sharing electron pairs describes covalent bonds, which form mainly between nonmetals.
n.1: Metallic bonding holds atoms of a metal together; NaCl is a metal combined with a nonmetal.
n.3: The bond is ionic, but the electron moves from the metal (sodium) to the nonmetal (chlorine), not the other way.

CH.q: Element X is in period 3, group 2, and element Y is in period 3, group 17. Based on periodic trends, which statement correctly compares X with Y?
o: X has the larger radius and the higher electronegativity
X has the larger radius and the lower ionization energy
X has the smaller radius and the lower electronegativity
X has the smaller radius and the higher ionization energy
CH.w: Step 1: X and Y are in the same period, and X is to the left. Step 2: Moving left across a period, radius increases while ionization energy and electronegativity decrease. So X (magnesium) is larger and has a lower ionization energy than Y (chlorine).

n.0: X is larger, but electronegativity is lower toward the left of a period, so X's is lower.
n.2: X's electronegativity is lower, but its radius is larger, not smaller, because it has fewer protons pulling on the same shells.
n.3: This reverses the trend. Elements toward the left of a period are larger and hold electrons less tightly.

CH.q: A jeweler cuts a solid gold bar into two unequal pieces. Which property of each piece is the same as that of the original, whole bar?
CH.w: Density is an intensive property: it does not depend on the amount of material. Each piece of gold has the same mass-to-volume ratio (about 19.3 g/cm³) as the whole bar.

n.1: Mass is an extensive property; each piece has less mass than the whole bar.
n.2: Volume is extensive; cutting the bar divides its volume between the pieces.
n.3: Surface area depends on the size and shape of a piece, so it changes when the bar is cut; it is not an intensive property.

CH.q: A sodium atom, atomic number 11, loses one electron during a reaction with chlorine and becomes the ion Na⁺. How many protons and electrons does the Na⁺ ion contain?
CH.w: Protons do not change in a chemical reaction, so Na⁺ keeps 11 protons. A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons; losing one leaves 10. Eleven positive charges and ten negative charges give a net charge of +1.

n.0: Twelve electrons would give a charge of 1-. A cation forms by losing electrons, not gaining them.
n.1: This removes a proton along with the electron. Protons stay fixed, and 10 protons with 10 electrons would be a neutral neon atom.
n.2: Ions differ from atoms in their electrons, not their protons; 10 protons would make the particle neon, not sodium.

CH.q: Which pair of atoms are isotopes of the same element?
CH.w: Isotopes have the same number of protons (the same element) but different numbers of neutrons. Both atoms have 8 protons (oxygen), with 8 and 10 neutrons: oxygen-16 and oxygen-18.

n.0: Both have a mass number of 16, but 8 and 7 protons make them different elements (oxygen and nitrogen).
n.2: 7 and 8 protons are different elements (nitrogen and oxygen), so these cannot be isotopes of one element.
n.3: These differ in electrons, not neutrons: the second is an ion (O²⁻), not an isotope.

CH.q: Glucose reacts completely with oxygen in a combustion-type reaction: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → ? Which products correctly complete the balanced equation?
CH.w: Complete combustion of a compound containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen produces carbon dioxide and water. Balancing: 6 C gives 6 CO₂, 12 H gives 6 H₂O, and 6 x 2 + 6 = 18 O atoms on the right match 6 + 12 = 18 on the left. The same overall equation describes cellular respiration.

n.0: This is balanced, but it leaves the oxygen unreacted; the products of complete combustion are CO₂ and H₂O.
n.2: This is balanced, but complete combustion forms CO₂, not carbon monoxide, and O₂ is consumed, not produced.
n.3: This is balanced, but hydrogen ends up as water, not H₂ gas, and oxygen gas is a reactant here, not a product.

CH.q: An opened bottle of soda goes flat much faster when it is left on a hot porch than when it is kept in a refrigerator. Which statement best explains this?
o: Gases are more soluble in warmer liquids
Warming raises the gas pressure above the soda
Heat breaks the dissolved CO₂ into C and O₂
Gases are less soluble in warmer liquids
CH.w: Unlike most solids, gases become less soluble as temperature rises. Warm soda can hold less dissolved carbon dioxide, so the gas escapes faster and the drink goes flat.

n.0: This reverses the rule for gases; more soluble gas would keep the soda fizzy longer when warm.
n.1: Higher gas pressure above a liquid would force more gas into solution, not less (Henry's law).
n.2: Warming a drink does not decompose carbon dioxide; the CO₂ simply comes out of solution as a gas.

CH.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a nuclear reaction from an ordinary chemical reaction?
o: It speeds up sharply when the sample is heated
It can change one element into another
It rearranges the valence electrons of atoms
It keeps every atom's proton count unchanged
CH.w: Nuclear reactions change the nucleus itself, so the number of protons can change and one element can become another (transmutation). Chemical reactions only rearrange electrons, so elements never change.

n.0: Radioactive decay rates (half-lives) are not changed by heating; chemical reaction rates are.
n.2: Rearranging valence electrons is what chemical reactions do; nuclear reactions change the nucleus.
n.3: Keeping the proton count unchanged describes a chemical reaction; alpha and beta decay change it.

CH.q: A technician dissolves 0.50 mol of KCl in enough water to make 250 mL of solution. What is the molarity?
CH.w: Molarity = moles ÷ liters of solution. 250 mL = 0.250 L, so 0.50 ÷ 0.250 = 2.0 M.

n.0: 0.13 M multiplies moles by liters (0.50 × 0.250); molarity divides.
n.1: 0.0020 M divides by 250 mL without converting to liters.
n.2: 0.50 M ignores the volume, treating the solution as 1 L.

CH.q: For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, 3.0 mol of H₂ is mixed with 2.0 mol of O₂. Which reactant runs out first, and how much water can form?
o: H₂ runs out; 3.0 mol of H₂O
O₂ runs out; 2.0 mol of H₂O
H₂ runs out; 1.5 mol of H₂O
O₂ runs out; 4.0 mol of H₂O
CH.w: 3.0 mol H₂ needs only 1.5 mol O₂ (2 : 1), and 2.0 mol is available, so H₂ is the limiting reactant. H₂ : H₂O is 2 : 2, so 3.0 mol H₂O forms.

n.1: O₂ is in excess: only 1.5 of its 2.0 mol react.
n.2: H₂ does limit, but the H₂ : H₂O ratio is 2 : 2, so 3.0 mol of water forms; 1.5 mol is the O₂ used.
n.3: 2.0 mol O₂ would need 4.0 mol H₂, but only 3.0 mol is present, so O₂ is in excess.

PH.q: An elevator motor lifts a 500 kg load 12 m in 20 s at constant speed. Using g = 10 m/s², what is its average power output?

n.1: Leaves out the height: 500 x 10 / 20 = 250.
n.2: 60,000 J is the work done; power divides it by the time.
n.3: Leaves out g: 500 x 12 / 20 = 300.

PH.q: A student can read her textbook clearly but cannot see the whiteboard at the front of the room. Which condition does she have, and which lens corrects it?
PH.w: Clear near vision with blurry distance vision is nearsightedness (myopia). A concave (diverging) lens corrects it.

n.0: Farsighted people see distant objects well; she sees near objects well.
n.1: She sees near objects well, so she is nearsighted, not farsighted.
n.2: Nearsightedness is right, but a converging lens corrects farsightedness.

PH.q: Light enters a plastic with an index of refraction of 1.5. Using c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s, what is the speed of light in the plastic? (n = c/v)

n.0: Multiplies c by n; light slows down in a material.
n.2: Divides c by 2 instead of by the index of 1.5.
n.3: 3.0 × 10^8 m/s is the speed in a vacuum; light is slower in plastic.

PH.q: A block of wood with a density of 700 kg/m³ floats in fresh water (1,000 kg/m³). What fraction of its volume is below the waterline?
PH.w: Fraction submerged = ρ_object / ρ_fluid = 700 / 1,000 = 0.70 = 70%.

n.0: 30% is the fraction above the waterline.
n.1: Half would be submerged only for a density of 500 kg/m³.
n.2: A block less dense than water floats partly above the surface.

PH.q: A sound at 70 dB is compared with a sound at 50 dB. How many times greater is the intensity of the louder sound?
PH.w: Each +10 dB multiplies intensity by 10. A 20 dB difference is two steps: 10 x 10 = 100 times.

n.0: Divides 70 by 50; decibel levels are not compared as a simple ratio.
n.1: Treats the 20 dB difference as a 20-fold change; decibels are logarithmic.
n.2: Treats 20 dB as a doubling; each 10 dB step is a tenfold change.

PH.q: A lab centrifuge rotor turns 50 times each second. What are its frequency and period?
PH.w: Frequency = revolutions per second = 50 Hz. Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 50 = 0.020 s.

n.0: Swaps frequency and period.
n.2: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, not equal to it.
n.3: Slips a decimal place in 1 / 50.

PH.q: An ambulance with its siren on approaches a pedestrian, passes her and drives away. What does she hear?
o: A lower pitch as it nears, then a higher pitch
The siren's true pitch, growing louder then softer
A higher pitch both as it nears and as it leaves
A higher pitch as it nears, then a lower pitch
PH.w: Doppler effect: a source moving toward an observer is heard at a higher frequency, and a source moving away at a lower frequency.

n.0: Reverses the Doppler effect; approaching raises the pitch.
n.1: Loudness does change, but so does the heard pitch: higher, then lower.
n.2: The pitch drops once the ambulance moves away.

PH.q: Two small charged spheres repel each other with a force of 16 N. If the distance between them is doubled, what is the new force?
PH.w: Coulomb's law is inverse-square: doubling r divides the force by 2² = 4. 16 / 4 = 4.0 N.

n.0: Multiplies by 2; a greater distance weakens the force.
n.2: Uses 1/r instead of 1/r²; doubling the distance quarters the force.
n.3: Multiplies by 4; the factor is right but the force must decrease.

PH.q: A book rests on a table. According to Newton's third law, what is the reaction force to Earth's gravitational pull on the book?
o: The book's gravitational pull on Earth
The book's downward push on the table
The table's upward push on the book
The floor's upward push on the table
PH.w: Third-law pairs are the same type of force acting on two different objects: Earth pulls the book down, so the book pulls Earth up with an equal force.

n.1: This is a contact force; its partner is the table's push on the book, not Earth's gravity.
n.2: The table's push balances the book's weight, but both act on the book, so they are not a third-law pair.
n.3: That push acts on the table and is a contact force; Earth's pull on the book pairs with the book's pull on Earth.

PH.q: Resistors of 4.0 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series to a 40 V battery. What is the voltage across the 10 Ω resistor?
PH.w: Series total R = 4.0 + 6.0 + 10 = 20 Ω. I = 40 / 20 = 2.0 A (the same through each). V across 10 Ω = 2.0 x 10 = 20 V.

n.0: 40 V is the whole battery voltage; series resistors share it.
n.2: Splits the voltage equally (40 / 3); series voltages divide in proportion to resistance.
n.3: 2.0 A is the current, not the voltage across the resistor.

PH.q: A 5.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 500 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
PH.w: Total momentum starts at zero. Bullet p = 0.020 x 500 = 10 kg·m/s, so the rifle has 10 kg·m/s backward: v = 10 / 5.0 = 2.0 m/s.

n.1: Divides the bullet's speed by the rifle's mass (500 / 5.0) and leaves out the bullet's mass.
n.2: Inverts the division (5.0 / 10).
n.3: Slips a decimal: uses 0.20 kg for the bullet (0.20 x 500 / 5.0).

PH.q: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 20 m/s is caught and stopped in 0.25 s. What average force does the glove exert on the ball?
PH.w: Change in momentum = 0.50 x 20 = 10 kg·m/s. Impulse F t = change in p, so F = 10 / 0.25 = 40 N.

n.0: Multiplies the momentum change by the time (10 x 0.25) instead of dividing.
n.1: Divides the speed by the time (20 / 0.25) and leaves out the mass.
n.2: 10 kg·m/s is the change in momentum, not the force.

PH.q: Which list ranks the speed of sound from fastest to slowest?
PH.w: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases: steel, water, air.

n.0: Liquids carry sound faster than gases.
n.1: Solids carry sound faster than liquids.
n.2: Reverses the order; sound is slowest in gases.

PH.q: A 2.0 kg ball and a 6.0 kg ball are released together from the same height in a vacuum chamber. How does the acceleration of the 6.0 kg ball compare with that of the 2.0 kg ball?
PH.w: In free fall with no air resistance every object accelerates at g, whatever its mass, so the accelerations are equal and the balls land together.

n.0: Inverts the mass ratio; mass does not change free-fall acceleration.
n.1: Squares the mass ratio; mass does not change free-fall acceleration.
n.3: Assumes heavier objects fall faster in proportion to mass; mass cancels in free fall.

PH.q: Which change to a copper wire lowers its resistance?
o: Using a thicker wire of the same length
Using a thinner wire of the same length
Heating the wire to a higher temperature
Using a longer wire of the same thickness
PH.w: Resistance falls as cross-sectional area rises: a thicker wire offers more paths for current.

n.1: A thinner wire has more resistance.
n.2: A metal's resistance rises with temperature.
n.3: Resistance rises with length.

PH.q: A child rides a carousel horse that moves in a circle at a constant speed. What is the direction of the horse's acceleration?
o: Away from the center of the circle
There is none, since its speed is constant
Toward the center of the circle
Along the tangent, in the direction of motion
PH.w: In uniform circular motion the velocity keeps changing direction, so the object accelerates toward the center (centripetal acceleration).

n.0: Centripetal means center-seeking; the outward 'centrifugal' feeling is inertia, not an acceleration.
n.1: Constant speed is not constant velocity; the changing direction is an acceleration.
n.3: A tangential acceleration would change the speed, which stays constant here.

PH.q: A negatively charged balloon is held near a small piece of neutral paper, and the paper jumps toward it. Why?
o: The balloon transfers protons to the paper
Like charges attract at very short range
The paper already carries a hidden positive charge
The balloon polarizes the paper and attracts it
PH.w: The balloon's negative charge pushes the paper's electrons slightly away, leaving the near side positive. The nearer positive side is attracted more strongly than the far side is repelled.

n.0: Protons do not move between objects; the balloon's field shifts the paper's electrons.
n.1: Like charges repel at every distance.
n.2: The paper is neutral; the attraction comes from charge separation within it.

PH.q: A delivery van travels along a straight, level highway at a constant 25 m/s. Which statement about the forces on the van is correct?
o: The forward force is larger than the drag
A net forward force keeps it moving
The drag is larger than the forward force
The net force on the van is zero
PH.w: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by F_net = m a the forces are balanced and the net force is zero (Newton's first law).

n.0: A forward force larger than drag would make the van speed up.
n.1: An object at constant velocity needs no net force to keep moving.
n.2: Drag larger than the forward force would give a net backward force and slow the van down.

PH.q: When the biceps contracts to flex the elbow and lift a cup held in the hand, which describes the lever?
PH.w: The elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps pulls on the forearm between the elbow and the hand (effort in the middle) and the cup is the load: a third-class lever. The effort arm is much shorter than the load arm, so the mechanical advantage is below 1; the forearm gains speed and range of motion instead.

n.0: A first-class lever has the fulcrum between the effort and the load; the elbow is at one end of the forearm.
n.1: In a second-class lever the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort; here the cup is at the far end of the forearm.
n.2: Right class, but the biceps attaches close to the elbow, so the effort arm is shorter than the load arm and the mechanical advantage is below 1.

PH.q: The same net force acts on a 3.0 kg cart and on a 12 kg cart. How does the acceleration of the 3.0 kg cart compare with that of the 12 kg cart?
PH.w: a = F / m. With the same force, a is inversely proportional to mass: 12 / 3.0 = 4, so the lighter cart accelerates 4 times as much.

n.0: Equal force does not mean equal acceleration when the masses differ.
n.2: Squares the mass ratio; a = F / m is a simple inverse relationship.
n.3: Treats acceleration as directly proportional to mass; it is inversely proportional.

PH.q: A stone is dropped from rest off a bridge. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how fast is it falling after 4.0 s?
PH.w: From rest, v = g t = 10 x 4.0 = 40 m/s.

n.1: 80 is the distance fallen in meters (1/2 x 10 x 16), not the speed.
n.2: Divides g by t (10 / 4.0) instead of multiplying.
n.3: Squares the time (10 x 4.0²); speed grows linearly with time in free fall.

PH.q: A train moves at a constant 72 km/h. How far does it travel in 15 s? (1 m/s = 3.6 km/h)
PH.w: Convert first: 72 km/h / 3.6 = 20 m/s. Then d = v t = 20 x 15 = 300 m.

n.0: Converts correctly but slips a decimal place (20 x 1.5).
n.1: Multiplies 72 by 15 without converting km/h to m/s.
n.2: Multiplies by 3.6 instead of dividing (72 x 3.6 = 259 m/s), then by 15.

PH.q: A bar magnet is cut in half across its middle. What results?
o: One piece with a north pole, one with a south pole
Two pieces of iron with no magnetic poles
One magnet and one unmagnetized piece
Two magnets, each with a north and a south pole
PH.w: Magnetic poles always come in pairs. Each piece becomes a smaller magnet with its own north and south pole.

n.0: Isolated north or south poles do not exist; each piece has both.
n.1: The pieces stay magnetized; cutting does not remove the poles.
n.2: Both pieces stay magnetized, each with a north and a south pole.

PH.q: A brick slides across a floor first on its large face, then on its narrow edge. In the simple friction model, how does the kinetic friction compare?
o: It depends on the sliding speed
PH.w: In the simple model f = μN: friction depends on the surfaces (μ) and the normal force, not on contact area or speed. The brick's weight is the same either way.

n.0: A smaller area does not change friction; the normal force is unchanged.
n.1: Kinetic friction in the simple model does not depend on speed.
n.3: Contact area does not change friction in the simple model.

PH.q: On a position-time graph, a cart's line is straight and slopes steadily upward. What does this show about the cart's motion?
o: It speeds up at a constant rate
It slows down at a constant rate
It is at rest at a fixed position
It moves at a constant velocity
PH.w: The slope of a position-time graph is velocity. A straight line has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant.

n.0: Reads the slope of a position-time graph as acceleration; speeding up would make the line curve upward.
n.1: Slowing down would make the line curve and flatten, not stay straight.
n.2: A cart at rest gives a horizontal line, not a rising one.

PH.q: Which statement about an ideal hydraulic lift is correct?
o: It multiplies energy, so less work is put in
It multiplies force; the small piston moves farther
It multiplies force and the work done
It multiplies force; the large piston moves farther
PH.w: Pascal's principle transmits the pressure, so the large piston gets a large force. Work in = work out, so the small piston must move a longer distance.

n.0: Energy is conserved; hydraulics cannot multiply energy.
n.2: A hydraulic lift multiplies force, not work.
